tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing Tools and Setup. This is where we get our tool ready before we learn. Our tool is called ScratchJr. It is an app on a tablet — and an app is a program, a set of steps a computer follows. By the end, you will have ScratchJr open and ready, and you will know that you used a tablet, which is a computer! You need a tablet with ScratchJr on it, and a grown-up nearby to help you find the app. There are 4 small steps. Step 1: Find the tablet and hold it in your hands. Look at it. It is flat, and you touch it with your finger. That is why we call it a tablet — and a tablet is a computer! Tell me when you have the tablet, and say one thing you notice about it. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for our lesson: Computers Are Everywhere. 🙂

This lesson has five big ideas. We will take them one at a time, like steps on a ladder. By the end, you will be able to point at things around you and say "that is a computer!" You only need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. Here is what I expect from you: after each step, tell me your answer in your own words. Even one word is fine. Do not worry about mistakes — mistakes are how we learn. Step 1 of 5. A computer is a clever machine that helps us do things. Computers are all around us — at home, at school, in a car, even in a watch. Look around the room you are in right now. Can you see one thing you think is a computer? Tell me what it is.

words.label: Computing Words
words.text:
Welcome! Today we are learning our Computing Words. 📚

These are the special words we use in this unit, like computer and laptop. We learn them so you can name the machines you see every day and tell someone what they do. Here is what I expect from you: say each word out loud, tell me what it means in your own words, then make your own sentence with it. That is what a really good answer looks like. We will do three words first. Ready? Let's start with something small. Step 1: The word is computer. Say it with me, slowly: com-pu-ter. A computer is a clever machine that helps us do things. Now you try: tell me one computer you can see in your home.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today we are doing "Circle the Computers". A computer is a clever machine that helps us do things. In this activity you look at some pictures and find the computers. We do it so you can spot computers all around you — at home, at school, everywhere. You need your activity page (or paper) and a pencil. Your grown-up can sit with you if you like. Here is what I expect: for each thing, you tell me yes it is a computer, or no it is not — and say why in a few words. There are five things, so five little steps. Here comes number one: a tablet. 📱

Is a tablet a computer? Tell me yes or no, and why.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are starting Unit 1: Computers Are Everywhere. This page is our Unit Overview. That means we look at the whole unit before we begin, like looking at a map before a trip. By the end of this unit you will be able to spot computers all around you, name four kinds of computers, and say what we put into a computer. You do not need a computer for this — just your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. What I expect from you: talk to me after each step. Even a short answer is perfect. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Look around the room you are in right now. Find one thing you think is a computer, and tell me what it is.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is just a way of working — the same steps a computer scientist uses. Our big idea is "Computers are everywhere." By the end you will be able to say that idea in your own words and find a real computer near you. You need your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are 4 steps. I will give you one at a time, and I will wait for you. Step 1: Tell me what a computer is, in your own words. You do not have to use fancy words. A good answer says it is a machine that helps us do things. Off you go — what is a computer?

code.label: Code Examples
code.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher today. 👋

This page is called Code Examples. In Unit 1 we don't type code yet — we learn the idea behind it. A program (an app) is just a list of steps a computer follows. So we will play a game where I am the computer and you write the steps. By the end you will be able to say what a program is, and write a tiny program of your own. You just need your voice, and a pencil if you like. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Tell me the name of one app you use on a phone or tablet, and what job it does. A good answer is two things: the app, and its job. For example, "a game app — it plays games."

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Visual Models page. A visual model is a picture that shows a big idea. We have five little picture cards here. Each one shows something about computers. We do this so the ideas stick in your head as pictures, not just words. Here is what I expect from you. Look at each card, then tell me the idea in YOUR own words. Short is fine. One or two sentences is perfect. You will need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. Five cards, five steps. Step 1. Look at the first card: "Computers are everywhere."

Now look around the room you are in. Can you find one computer near you? Tell me what it is. 😊

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a question with a good answer shown next to it. We look at one together, then you say it in your own words. That is how the words stick in your head. By the end you will be able to say what a computer is, name the four kinds of computers, and tell me what an app does. All you need is your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are 5 short steps. Here comes step one. Step one: A phone is a computer. True or false? Say "true" or "false", and then tell me why in a few words. That is what a good answer looks like.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Welcome! I'm your teacher today. 😊

This is Guided Practice. That means we practise the big ideas from Unit 1 together, one small question at a time. Why we do it: practice helps the new words stick in your brain — words like computer, laptop, app and keyboard. By the end, you will be able to name computers, say what a program is, and name a thing that puts words into a computer. What you need: just your voice, and your thinking brain. A pencil and paper if you like. What I expect from you: try each one yourself first, and answer in a full sentence. Guessing is fine! Mistakes are how we learn. There are 6 questions. Here comes question one. Which one is a computer — a tablet, or a banana?

activities.label: Build It
activities.text: Hello! Today we are doing "Circle the Computers". A computer is a clever machine that helps us do things. In this activity you look at some things and pick out the computers. We do this so your eyes get good at spotting computers all around you. You need a pencil and paper, or just your voice to tell me. There are 5 things to look at, one at a time. I expect one answer each time: computer, or not a computer. Say why in a few words if you can. Here comes number one! A tablet. Is a tablet a computer, yes or no?

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Debug It. To debug means to find a mistake and fix it. On this page the mistakes are not in a machine — they are little mix-ups about computers. Lots of children believe them! Your job is to be the detective who spots the mix-up and says the true thing instead. There are four mix-ups. I will give you one at a time. I expect you to tell me if it is true or not true, and then say the true idea in your own words. Take your time — there's no rush. Here comes mix-up number one:

"Only the big machine on a desk is a computer."

Is that true, or not true? 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are on the Games page. These games are little practice rounds about Unit 1: Computers Are Everywhere. We play them so the new words stick in your head — computer, desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone, app and input device. By the end, you will be able to answer quick questions about computers without stopping to think hard. What I expect from you: try your own answer first, even if you are not sure. A guess with a reason is a brilliant answer. If you get one wrong, that is fine — mistakes are how we learn. You need nothing but your eyes and your thinking brain. 🙂

There are 4 rounds in our first game, called Quick Match. I will give you one round at a time. Here comes question one. True or False: a phone is a computer.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Word Wall — our Quick Reference. It holds all the important words from Unit 1, like computer, laptop and keyboard. We are doing this so the words stick in your head, and so you can say them out loud all by yourself. By the end, you will be able to name three computer words and use them in your own sentences. You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want to say things to them too. There are 4 steps. Step 1: Look at your page and find the word "computer". Now tell me, in your own words, what a computer is. It does not need to be perfect — just tell me what you think. 😊

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Welcome to Computing Fluency! This is our quick-answer game. I will ask you short questions about computers. You answer as best you can. It helps the words stick in your head, so you remember them fast. Here is what I expect from you: try to answer in a full sentence, like "A tablet is a computer." And it is fine to think for a moment first. There are 6 questions. You just need your voice or your typing fingers. Here comes question one. Which one is a computer — a tablet, or a banana?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Lovely — let's do this one together! 😊

This activity is called Solve Real Problems. I will ask you little questions about computers in real places — at home, at school, at the market. It helps you use what you have learned in real life, not just on the page. By the end, you will be able to spot a computer anywhere you go! You need just your voice or your typing. No pencil needed. There are 4 questions. What I expect from you: try your best answer, and if you can, tell me a tiny bit of why. Being wrong is fine — mistakes are how we learn. Here comes question one. This one is about home. A phone is a computer. True or False?

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Welcome! Today we are learning how to stay safe when we use a computer. Computers are everywhere, so we need to know some safety rules. Just like we look both ways before we cross the road! There are three safety rules to learn. By the end, you will be able to say them in your own words. You just need your listening ears and your voice. A grown-up nearby can help too. Here comes step one. Rule one: Check before you trust. Anyone can put anything on the internet. So not everything you read is true. If it is important, check on another website, and ask a grown-up you trust. Now you try. Can you tell me this rule in your own words? Even one short sentence is great.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Explain Your Thinking". In this activity you say your answers out loud or type them, and then you tell me WHY. Talking about why helps the idea stick in your brain. By the end, you will be able to name computer words and explain them in your own words. You just need your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if you want help typing. There are four short questions. I will give you one at a time. Here comes question one. What is another name for a program? Is it an app, or a chair? Tell me your answer, and then tell me why you chose it. 😊

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Today we are doing our Unit Challenge. It is called My Computer Scrapbook. You will make one special page that shows all four kinds of computer, and then go on a computer hunt around your home. We do this so you can show everything you have learned in Unit 1 — and so you can point at a computer and say its name all by yourself. You will need paper, a pencil, and colours if you have them. A grown-up can help you. There are 5 steps. I will give you one at a time. 😊

Step 1: Fold or draw lines on your paper to make 4 boxes. Two boxes on top, two boxes underneath. What I expect: 4 empty boxes, big enough to draw inside. Tell me when your boxes are ready!

project.label: Unit Project
project.text:
Hello! Today you are making your Computer Scrapbook. 📓

It is a little book of pictures you make yourself. You will draw the four kinds of computer, then go on a computer hunt around your home. We do this so you can see and name computers all by yourself. You need paper, a pencil, and colours if you have them. A grown-up can help you fold the paper. There are five steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Take your paper. Draw four big empty boxes on it, like four windows. Number them 1, 2, 3, 4. Tell me when your four boxes are ready!

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Welcome to Unit 2! It is called "Be an Animator". An animator is a person who makes pictures move, like in a cartoon. In this unit you will learn how to tell a computer, step by step, how to make a character move — and then you will really do it! Today, on this page, we are getting ready. We will look at what you will learn, the new words, and the tool you will use. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are 4 little steps. Step 1. Look at the words "Be an Animator" at the top of your page. Tell me: what do you think an animator does? Just guess — any idea is a good idea. 😊

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text:
Hello! Today we are getting our tools ready. This page is called Tools and Setup. Before an animator can make a character move, they need their tools open and working. Our tool is called ScratchJr. It is an app with coloured picture blocks, made for children your age. By the end, you will have ScratchJr open with a brand new project, ready to make something move. What I expect from you: you tap carefully, you tell me when each step is done, and you say "I'm stuck" if something looks different. A grown-up can sit with you and help. 🙂

There are 4 steps. Here is step 1. Find a tablet and look for the ScratchJr app. It has an orange face on it. Tap it once to open it. Tell me when it is open — or tell me if you cannot find it.

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Welcome to our Computing Words page! Today we learn the special words animators use. Words like algorithm and code are the words you need for everything else in this unit. By the end you will be able to say each word and tell me what it means in your own words. You need your voice, and a pencil if you want to write. We will do it in three steps: first three words, then the rest, then a little check. Here comes step one. Our first word is algorithm. An algorithm is a set of steps for a job, in the right order. Like the steps to wash your hands: tap on, soap, scrub, rinse, dry. Say the word out loud with me, slowly: al-go-rithm. Then tell me one job you do at home that has steps. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Welcome to our lesson! Today you are an animator. An animator is someone who makes pictures move. We will learn how to give steps to a computer, so a character moves how we want. By the end, you will know the word algorithm, and you will be able to make a character move on a screen. You need a pencil, some paper, and your voice for saying steps out loud. A tablet with ScratchJr later, if you have one. There are five parts. Here is part one. Stand up. Pretend to wash your hands in the air. Say each step out loud as you do it: turn on the tap, get the soap, scrub scrub scrub, rinse, dry. I expect you to say all five steps out loud, in that order, with big happy actions. 🧼

Tell me when you have done it!

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today we are going to be step detectives. 🕵️

This activity is called Put the Steps in Order. You will look at the steps for washing your hands, but they are all mixed up! Your job is to put them in the right order, 1, 2, 3. Why do we do this? Because a set of steps for a job, in the right order, has a special name — an algorithm. Computers need algorithms too! What I expect from you: think carefully, and tell me your order in your own words. It is fine to get it wrong the first time. Mistakes are how we learn. You need: your activity page (or paper), and a pencil. There are 3 steps in this activity. Here comes step one. Look at these three mixed-up steps and read them out loud to me:

Dry your hands
Turn on the tap and wet your hands
Scrub with soap

Tell me when you have read them all. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Visual Models activity. Visual models are picture helpers. Each picture shows one big idea from "Be an Animator". We look at each picture and say the idea in our own words. That is how the idea sticks in your head. Here is what I expect from you: look, think, then tell me in your own words. Short words are fine. Guessing is fine too — mistakes are how we learn. There are 5 pictures. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Look at the first model on your page. It is called "Everyday steps". It shows the steps for washing your hands. Tell me one step you do when you wash your hands. Just one! 🧼

code.label: Code Examples
code.text: Welcome, animator! Today we are reading code together. Code is the blocks that tell a computer what to do. On this page you will see short lists of blocks. Our job is to read each block and say out loud what it makes the character do. By the end, you will be able to look at a set of blocks and know what will happen before you even press the green flag. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. There are 4 steps. Step 1. Look at the first code example on your page. It starts with a yellow block called Start on Green Flag. Tell me: what do you think that block does? Take your time — there's no rush.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are learning the Method for this unit. A method is a way of working. It is the same four steps we use every time we learn something new in Computing. We will use it on our first big idea: an algorithm, which means a set of steps for a job, in the right order. By the end, you will be able to say what an algorithm is in your own words, and try one yourself. You will need your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like. There are 4 steps. Here is step one. Step 1: Say the idea in your own words. Tell me what an algorithm is, using your own words. It does not have to be perfect. A good answer says something about steps and about order. Off you go — I am listening. 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Lovely! Let's get started together. This is our Guided Practice. It is six little questions about Unit 2, Be an Animator. We do it so the big words stick in your head: algorithm, order, code. What I expect from you: try each one out loud or type it, even if you are not sure. A guess is fine! Try to answer in a full sentence when you can. You need nothing but your thinking brain. Here comes question one. What is an algorithm? Is it a set of steps, a kind of food, or a big animal?

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Welcome to our Quick Reference page! This page is our word box for Unit 2, "Be an Animator". It holds the special words we use when we make a character move. We do this so the words feel easy in your mouth, not scary. By the end you will know what each word means and be able to use it in your own sentence. You just need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one! Step 1: Let's learn three words together. algorithm — a set of steps for a job, in the right order. Like the steps to wash your hands. step — one thing you do. Like "turn on the tap". order — which step comes first, next and last. Read them slowly. Then tell me: which of these three words feels the trickiest to you?

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Let's do this together. 😊

This page is called Worked Examples. That means we look at a question, try it, and then see how a good answer looks. We do this so you get really good at algorithms — steps for a job, in the right order. Here is what I expect from you: try each one first, even if you are not sure. Then tell me your answer in a few words. Guessing bravely is allowed! Mistakes are how we learn. There are six little examples. We will do one at a time. Here comes question one. Think about washing your hands. Does the order of the steps matter? Yes or no?

activities.label: Build It
activities.text: Welcome to Build It! Today you are the animator. That means you make a character move on the screen, all by yourself. We do this because a computer only moves when we give it steps. Those steps are called code. By the end, your character will move across and hop when you tap the green flag. You need a tablet with ScratchJr open. A grown-up can sit with you to help. There are 5 small steps. Here is step 1. Open ScratchJr. Tap the plus sign to start a new project. I expect to see an empty white stage with a cat on it, and coloured blocks at the bottom. Tell me when your new project is open! 🐱

games.label: Games
games.text:
Welcome to our Games page! 🎮

Today we are playing the game called Quick Match. It is a game about our big word: algorithm — a set of steps for a job, in the right order. We play games because practising the words makes them stick in your brain. There are 4 questions in this game. Here is what I expect from you: read each question, think for a moment, then tell me your answer in your own words. Guessing is fine — mistakes are how we learn. You need your tablet or computer with the Games page open, and your thinking brain. Ready? Here comes question one. An algorithm is... a set of steps, a kind of food, or a big animal?

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Welcome to Debug It! Let me tell you what we are doing today. A bug is a little mistake in our steps. Debug means we find the mistake and fix it. Today you are a Debug Detective, and we have four little problems to solve together. Why do we do this? Because every animator's blocks go wrong the first time. Every programmer's code fails the first time. Finding the bug is a real computing skill! What I expect from you: look carefully, tell me what is silly or wrong, and say it in your own words. You do not have to be right straight away. Good detectives take their time. Here comes bug number one. Someone said: "The order does not matter."
So they got dressed like this. First they put their shoes on. Then they put their socks on top of their shoes! What is wrong here? Tell me in your own words. 🕵️

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Computing Fluency. Fluency means quick practice. We answer small questions about our unit words so they stick in your head. By the end you will remember what an algorithm is and what the ScratchJr blocks do. You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. No pencil needed! Here is what I expect: try each question yourself first, and answer in a full sentence if you can. Wrong answers are fine — mistakes are how we learn. There are 6 questions. Here comes question one. What is an algorithm? Is it a set of steps, a kind of food, or a big animal?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Solve Real Problems page. On this page you get little problems from real life — home, school, the market. You use what you learned about algorithms and code to answer them. This helps you see that steps are everywhere, not just on a screen. There are 4 problems. I will give you one at a time. What I expect from you: think first, then tell me your answer in a full sentence. Guessing is fine — mistakes are how we learn! You need your eyes, your brain, and maybe a pencil. Ready? Here comes question one. It is a home problem. Put these three steps in the right order. Say which is 1, which is 2, which is 3. Dry your hands
Get the soap
Scrub your hands

Take your time — there's no rush.

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello! Today we are learning something very important: how to stay safe online. When we use a tablet or a computer, we need two safe habits. One: tell a grown-up if something worries you. Two: respect other people's work. By the end, you will be able to say both safety rules in your own words. All you need is your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. There are 3 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look at the first rule on your page — "Tell someone if something worries you." Read it, or ask your grown-up to read it with you. Then tell me: who is one grown-up YOU would tell if something on a tablet made you feel worried? A good answer names a real person, like "my mum" or "my teacher". Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! I'm your teacher today. This page is called Explain Your Thinking. That means you don't just pick an answer — you tell me WHY, in your own words. We do this because saying an idea out loud helps it stick in your brain, like glue! Here is what I expect from you: try to answer in a full sentence, and use our special words when you can — algorithm, step, order, code, program, block. There are four questions. We will do one at a time. Take your time — there's no rush. Here comes question one. What do we call the blocks that tell a computer what to do? Is it code, soap, or a nap?

project.label: Unit Project
project.text:
Welcome to your Unit Project — Be an Animator! 🎬

In this project you make your very own moving character, like a cartoon maker does. We do it to show that you can put steps in the right order and turn them into code. By the end, your character will move, hop and even talk! You need a tablet with ScratchJr, and a pencil and paper for planning. Here is what I expect from you: put your blocks in the right order, join them in a row with no gaps, and be ready to tell me what happens when you tap the green flag. There are 5 steps. Ready? Here comes step one. Step 1: On your paper, write or draw the steps for your character. It should move across, then hop. Put them in order like this: Start, then Move Right, then Hop, then End. Tell me when your plan is written, and read your order back to me. Take your time — there's no rush.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is your Unit Challenge: Be an Animator. You are going to make a character really move on the screen — you become the animator! We do this so you can show that you know an algorithm (steps for a job, in the right order) and can turn it into code. You will need a pencil and paper, and a tablet with ScratchJr. Here is what I expect from you: put the blocks in the right order, join them in a row with no gaps, and make your character move, hop and say "Hello!". There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: On your paper, write the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 next to these blocks to show the right order. Hop (2) — jump up (blue)
Start on Green Flag (yellow)
End — stop (red)
Move Right (5) — move across (blue)

Think: which block must come first, before anything can happen? Tell me your order when you are ready. Take your time — there's no rush.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Welcome, data detective! This unit is called Be a Data Detective. Data is a big word that just means information — numbers, words, pictures or sounds. We do this unit because data is all around you, and computers work with data all day long. By the end, you will be able to sort things into groups, count them, and make a little picture called a block graph. You need a pencil, some paper, and a small pile of things from home — blocks, buttons, crayons or toy cars. Ask your grown-up to help you find them if you like. There are 5 steps. I will give you one at a time, and I will wait for you each time. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Name a computing device. A computing device is a machine that works with data. It can answer our questions. A phone, a tablet and a watch are all computing devices. I expect you to tell me ONE computing device you see at home, and one question it can answer for you. Tell me your answer when you are ready. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the lesson called "Be a Data Detective". In this lesson we learn about data. Data is just a nice word for information. By the end, you will be able to sort things into groups, count them, and read a little picture called a block graph. All you need is a pencil, some paper, and a few small things from around you, like toys or stones. There are 5 steps. I will give you one step at a time. Step 1: Data is all around us. Data can be numbers, words, pictures or sounds. A computing device is a machine that works with data — like a phone, a tablet or a watch. It can answer our questions. Here is what I expect from you: name one computing device you have seen at home or at school. Tell me when you are ready. 😊

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 😊

This page is called Tools and Setup. It is where we get ready before we start being a Data Detective. A data detective looks at information and finds answers. By the end of this page, you will have everything you need on your table. I expect three things from you: get each item, tell me when it is ready, and take your time. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step one: get a piece of paper and a pencil. Put them in front of you. Tell me "ready" when you have them.

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Welcome, detective! Today we are learning our Unit 3 Computing Words. These are the special words we use when we work with data. Learning them helps you talk like a real data detective. By the end you will be able to say each word and what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You need your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are six words. We will learn them three at a time, so it is nice and easy. Here comes word one: data. Data means information. It can be numbers, words, pictures or sounds. Like this: how many mangoes are in the bowl. That number is data! Now you try one. Tell me one thing at your home that is data. It could be a number, a picture, or a sound.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello, data detective! Today we are doing "What can it tell us?"

A computing device is a machine that works with data. Data is just a fancy word for information. In this activity you match each device to the question it can answer. By the end, you will know what different devices can tell us. You need a pencil and your activity page, or just a piece of paper. There are 3 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Write these three devices down the left side of your paper, one under the other. phone
watch
game

Tell me when you have written them. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are on the Visual Models page. Visual models are just pictures that show a big idea. Looking at a picture helps the idea stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to say, in your own words, what data means, what sorting means, and what a block graph shows. You need your eyes, your voice, and a pencil and paper nearby. There are five pictures, so five little steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Look at the first picture, the one called "Data is all around us". Look for a phone, a tablet or a watch in it. What I expect: you point at one machine you can see, and say its name out loud. Tell me which one you found. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello, data detective! Today we learn the Method — that means the steps we follow every time we work with data. 🕵️

Here is what it is: data is information, like how many mangoes are in a bowl. The Method has four steps: say the idea in your own words, copy an example, change one small thing and guess what happens, then check. Why we do it: so you can find answers all by yourself, like a real detective. What you need: just your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like. What I expect from you: try each step, tell me your answer, and it is fine to guess. Mistakes are how we learn. Step 1 of 4. Tell me in your own words: what is data?

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a問 — sorry, a question we solve together, step by step, so you can see how a data detective thinks. We are doing this so you get good at reading data and finding answers. By the end you will be able to look at a block graph and say which group has the most and which has the fewest. You need a pencil and a piece of paper. Nothing else! There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Look at our block graph. Each block is one child. Mango: ####
Banana: ##
Apple: ###

My question: which fruit did the MOST children like? What I expect from you: point along each row with your finger, see which row is the longest, then tell me the fruit name. Take your time — there's no rush.

code.label: Code Examples
code.text:
Hello, detective! Let's get started. This page is called Code Examples, but in Grade 1 we do our computing with a pencil, not a keyboard. So today I will teach you the real Unit 3 activity: Count the Fruit and Make a Block Graph. Here is why we do it. Data means information. When we sort things into groups and count them, we can see the answer to a question straight away. By the end, you will be able to count each group and colour a block graph, just like a real data detective. You need a sheet of paper, a pencil, and some colours if you have them. Ask your grown-up to help you find them. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Copy this basket of fruit onto your paper, or just look at it here:

🥭 🍌 🥭 🍎 🥭 🍌

Now touch each mango with your finger and count them out loud. Tell me how many mangoes you see.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello, detective! Today we practise being a Data Detective. We will read a block graph and answer questions about it. Data means information — like how many children like mango. This helps you count, sort and put things in order. You need a pencil and a paper, or just your voice. There are 6 little steps. Here is our graph. It is our class fruit data:

Mango: ####
Banana: ##
Apple: ###

I expect you to look, point and count carefully — one touch for each block. Take your time — there's no rush. Here comes question one. How many children liked mango? Count the blocks in the mango row and tell me the number.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Let's look at this page together. This page is our Word Box for Unit 3, "Be a Data Detective". It holds the six special words a data detective needs. We learn them so that when you sort your toys or count your snacks, you can say what you are doing like a real computer scientist. You will need your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby to listen. Here is what I expect from you: for each word, you say it out loud, then make your very own sentence with it. Your own sentence is the important part! We have five small steps. Here comes step one. Step one: our first word is data. Data means information. It can be numbers, words, pictures or sounds. For example, how many mangoes are in your bowl — that is data. A photo of your family is data too! Now say the word out loud: data. Then tell me one piece of data from your home. Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Hello, data detective! Today we build our very own fruit survey. 🍌

Here is what it is: we ask our friends or family which fruit they like best — mango, banana or apple. Their answers are our data. Data means information. Then we count and colour a block graph so we can SEE which fruit wins. You will need a pencil, some colours, and a sheet of paper. From me, I expect you to do each step yourself and tell me when you are done. Neat is nice, but trying is what matters most. There are 6 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Write our question at the top of your paper, or say it out loud if writing is tricky. The question is: "Which fruit do you like best — mango, banana or apple?" You can draw the three fruits under it too. Tell me when you have done step 1. 😊

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Welcome, data detective! 🕵️

This page is called Debug It. A bug is a little mistake in our thinking. Your job is to spot the mistake and fix it. We do this because fixing a mix-up makes the idea stick in your head much better than just reading it. There are 5 bugs. I will show you one at a time. You tell me if it is right or wrong, and why. Even a short answer like "no, because..." is perfect. You just need your voice and your thinking brain! Here comes bug number one. Someone says: "Data is only numbers."

Is that right or wrong? What do you think?

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello, data detective! Let's do Computing Fluency together. This activity is quick practice. I ask you short questions about data, and you answer fast. We do it so counting, sorting and ordering become easy for you, like tying your shoes. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil. There are 6 quick questions. What I expect from you: try your best guess, even if you are not sure. Mistakes are how we learn. Here comes question one. Our class made a block graph. Mango has 4 blocks. Banana has 2 blocks. Apple has 3 blocks. How many children liked mango?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello, detective! Today we are on the Solve Real Problems page. This is where you use your data detective skills on real things — at home, at school, at the market. You will sort things into groups, count them, and put numbers in order. By the end, you will be able to look at a muddle of things and say "this group belongs together!"

You need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking voice. There are four problems. I will give you one at a time. Here is problem one. It is a home problem. Look at these five things:
mango, banana, apple, ball, toy car

Some are fruit. Some are toys. Tell me which ones belong in the FRUIT group. I am looking for you to name every fruit — and leave the toys out. Take your time.

games.label: Games
games.text:
Welcome to the Games page! This is our fun practice part of Unit 3, Be a Data Detective. Each game gives you four quick questions about our data words, and you tap the answer you think is right. We do this because playing the words again and again makes them stick in your brain. By the end you will know what data, sort, group, count and order mean without stopping to think. You need: your screen, and your voice to tell me your answers. No pencil needed. 🕵️

There are 4 steps. Here is step 1. Before we play, let's warm up one word. Tell me in your own words: what does the word data mean?

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Welcome, data detective! This page is called Stay Safe Online. It has three safety rules for when we use a computing device — that is a machine that works with data, like a phone or a tablet. We learn these rules so you know what to do if something online feels wrong. By the end, you will be able to say all three rules in your own words. You just need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you have one. There are three steps — one rule each. Step 1: Check before you trust. Anyone can put anything on the internet. So not everything you see is true! If something looks important, we check it in another place, or we ask a grown-up. Here is what I expect from you: tell me one thing you could do if a website said "goats can fly". 🐐

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 😊

This page is called Explain Your Thinking. You look at some data, then you say your answer out loud AND say why. Saying why is the best part — it shows you are a real data detective. By the end, you will be able to read a block graph and explain your thinking in your own words. You need: your eyes, your voice, and a pencil if you want to write. There are 4 questions. Here comes question one. First, look at our block graph:

mango — 4 blocks
banana — 2 blocks
apple — 3 blocks

Question one: Which fruit did the FEWEST children like? "Fewest" means the smallest number. Look for the shortest row. Tell me the fruit, and tell me why you chose it. Take your time — there's no rush.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Welcome, data detective! 🕵️ Today's challenge is called "Our Favourite Fruit". You will ask people one question, collect their answers, and turn those answers into a picture called a block graph. That picture is made of data — data means information. By the end you will be able to look at your graph and say which fruit is the class favourite. You need a pencil, some paper, and a few people to ask — friends, or family at home. There are 5 steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Write your question at the top of your paper, or just say it out loud to me. The question is: "Which fruit do you like best — mango, banana or apple?"

A good step 1 has three choices only, so it is easy to count later. Tell me when your question is ready.

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Welcome, Data Detective! Today we do our Unit Project: "Our Favourite Fruit". A detective asks a question, collects the answers, and finds out the truth. Our answers are called data — that means information. By the end, you will have a block graph that shows which fruit your family or class likes best. You need a pencil, some paper, and a few people to ask. There are 5 steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Write your question at the top of your paper, or say it out loud: "Which fruit do you like best — mango, banana or apple?" Then draw three boxes on your paper, one for mango, one for banana, one for apple. Tell me when that is done. 🕵️

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are starting Unit 4: Be a Designer. This page is our unit tour. We look at what we will learn before we learn it, just like looking at a map before a trip. By the end of this tour you will know the big idea of the unit, three new words, and the app we will use. You need your listening ears, and a pencil and paper if you like writing things down. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: The big idea of this unit is: when we change the steps, we change what happens. Think about walking to your kitchen. If you take 3 steps, you stop in one place. If you take 10 steps, you stop somewhere else. You changed the steps, so you changed what happened! Now you try: tell me one thing you do with steps in order. Getting dressed? Brushing your teeth? Just tell me one. 🙂

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Tools and Setup page. This is where we get our coding tool ready. The tool is called ScratchJr. It is an app where you join coloured picture blocks to make a character move. We do this first so that later, when we build our Boat program, everything is ready and we can just play and learn. Here is what I expect from you: get a tablet or a computer, ask your grown-up to help if you need it, and tell me after each step when it is done. That is all. Take your time — there's no rush. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Find ScratchJr. On a tablet, ask your grown-up to open the app store and look for ScratchJr. On a computer, go to scratchjr.org. Done well looks like this: you can see the ScratchJr picture, an orange cat face. Tell me when you can see it. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and our lesson is called "Be a Designer". In this lesson we learn one big idea: when we change the steps, we change what happens. We do it because that is what real coders do — they give steps, then change them to make something better. By the end you will know what an algorithm is, and you will be able to make a character go fast or slow, near or far. You need your ears, your voice, and one finger for counting. A pencil and paper would be lovely too. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step one. Step one: the word algorithm. An algorithm is a set of steps for doing a job, in the right order. Think about washing your hands. We wet them, then soap them, then dry them. We never dry first! Now you try. Tell me the steps for brushing your teeth, in order. Two or three steps is perfect. I am looking for them to be in the right order.

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Computing Words. Computing Words are the special words we use in Unit 4, "Be a Designer". We learn them so that when I say "algorithm" or "predict", you know exactly what I mean. By the end, you will be able to say each word, tell me what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You just need your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper if you like writing. We will do this in 3 steps. We will learn three words first, then three more, then play a little quiz. Here is Step 1. Our first word is algorithm. An algorithm is a set of steps for doing a job, in the right order. Like getting ready for school: put on socks, then shoes. Not shoes then socks — that would be silly! Say the word with me, slowly: al-go-rithm. Now your turn. Tell me one algorithm you do at home. Just say the steps in order, like "first... then... then...". Two or three steps is perfect.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and our activity is called Follow the Frog. Here is what it is. A frog stands on stone 1. We give it one step: move right 3. You will count the hops and find where the frog lands. We do this because a step is one instruction, and steps in order make an algorithm. Counting hops helps you see that the steps decide what happens. You need a pencil, a piece of paper, and your counting finger. There are 3 steps, and I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Draw five stones in a row on your paper, like this:
[ 1 ] [ 2 ] [ 3 ] [ 4 ] [ 5 ]
Write the numbers 1 to 5 inside them, and draw a little frog sitting on stone 1. I am looking for five stones in a row, numbered in order, with the frog on stone 1. Tell me when it is done!

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 👩‍🏫

This page is called Visual Models. A visual model is just a picture that shows a big idea. We are doing this so the big ideas of Unit 4 stick in your head — pictures help us remember much better than words alone. Here is what I expect from you: look at each picture, then tell me the idea in YOUR own words. Short is fine. One or two sentences is a great answer. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are four steps. Step 1. Look at the first model on your page. It is called "Steps in order (what is an algorithm?)". Tell me: what do you think an algorithm is? Take your time — there's no rush.

code.label: Code Examples
code.text:
Welcome, designer! Today we are on the Code Examples page. Here we read little programs made of coloured blocks. Reading blocks means saying out loud what each block does. By the end, you will be able to look at blocks and guess what the character will do — before you even tap the green flag! You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are 4 short examples. We will do them one at a time. Here comes step one. Look at this program:

Start on Green Flag (yellow)
Set Speed: slow (orange)
Move Right (14) (blue)
End (red)

Read it to me one line at a time, out loud. Then tell me just this: which block makes the program start? I am hoping you say the yellow one and tell me why. Take your time — there's no rush.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a small question with the thinking shown. We do these so you can see how a designer thinks, one step at a time. By the end you will know how to make a character go further, faster, and in the right order. You need your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil. There are 6 examples. I expect you to say your answer AND tell me why — even one little reason is perfect. Here comes question one. Two frogs are hopping. Frog A moves 2 steps. Frog B moves 8 steps. Which frog goes further away from the start?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Learn the Method. A method is just a way of working. It is the same four steps that real program designers use. We will practise it with our first big idea: an algorithm, which means a set of steps in the right order. By the end you will be able to say what an algorithm is in your own words, and change one step to see what happens. You need: your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like. There are four steps. I will give you one at a time. Here comes step one. Step one: say the main idea in your own words. Think about washing your hands. You wet, you soap, you rub, you rinse, you dry. Those steps go in that order. So tell me: what is an algorithm? A whole sentence is perfect. Take your time — there's no rush.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 👋

This is our Guided Practice for Unit 4, "Be a Designer". We practise the big idea together: when we change the steps, we change what happens. By the end you will be able to read code blocks and say what a character will do. You just need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil. There are 5 little steps. I will give you one at a time. Here comes step 1. Two frogs start on the same line. Frog A moves 2 steps. Frog B moves 8 steps. Which frog goes further? Tell me A or B, and tell me why. Take your time — there's no rush.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are on the Quick Reference page. This page is our word box for Unit 4. It holds the special computing words we use when we make a character move. We do this so the words feel easy and friendly, not big and scary. By the end, you will be able to say what each word means in your own words. What I expect from you: say each word out loud, then tell me its meaning in YOUR words. Not perfect words — your words. You will need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1. Say this word out loud: algorithm. It means a set of steps for doing a job, in the right order. Now tell me: what are the steps you do to get ready for bed? Say them in order. 🌙

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Hello! Today you are a Program Designer. 🚢

In this activity we build a Boat that sails across the sea in ScratchJr. We do it so you can see the big idea of this unit: when we change the steps, we change what happens. What I expect from you: try each step yourself, and tell me when it is done. If something goes wrong, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. You need a tablet with ScratchJr open. There are 6 steps. Ready? Here is step 1. Step 1: Open ScratchJr. Tap the plus sign to start a new project. Tell me when you see your new empty page.

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Debug It. A bug is a little mistake in our steps. Debug means to find the mistake and fix it. We do this because every programmer's code fails the first time — and good designers know how to fix it. By the end, you will be able to spot five common bugs and say how to fix each one. You need: your eyes, your thinking, and a tablet with ScratchJr if you have one nearby. A pencil and paper is fine too. There are 5 bugs. Here comes bug one. Bug 1: "Fast means far."
A child thinks a fast character must go a long way too. What I expect from you: tell me in your own words — is that true or not true? And why? Take your time — there's no rush.

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Computing Fluency. Fluency means quick thinking. I ask you a short question, and you answer from what you know. It helps the Unit 4 words stick in your head, like algorithm, step and speed. There are 6 questions. I want you to try each one, even if you are not sure. A guess is fine here. Mistakes are how we learn. You only need your thinking brain. Ready? Here comes question one. What is an algorithm? Is it a set of steps, a kind of food, or a colour?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Solve Real Problems. Here is what it is. I will give you four little coding puzzles, one at a time. They use the things we learned about steps, blocks and speed. Why do we do it? Because a real designer has to think before they tap. This page helps you think like a designer. What I expect from you: try your best guess out loud (or type it), even if you are not sure. A guess is always allowed here. Mistakes are how we learn. You need your eyes, your brain, and maybe a pencil. Ready? Here comes question one, of four. Question 1. Put these three blocks in the right order. Write 1, 2 and 3. The blocks are: Move Right, End (Stop), Start on the Green Flag. Which one goes first? Tell me your order. 🐢

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Let's look at that together. This page is Games. These are little practice games about Unit 4, "Be a Designer". You tap an answer, and the game tells you if you got it. We play them so the big words — algorithm, step, speed, block — stick in your head like a song. What I expect from you: try your best guess, tell me your answer here, and don't worry about mistakes. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 3 steps. Here is step 1. Step 1: A warm-up from me, before we touch the page. What is an algorithm? Is it a set of steps, a kind of food, or a colour? Take your time — there's no rush.

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello! Today we are learning how to Stay Safe Online. Being safe online is just as important as knowing how to code. We do this because you use tablets and computers. There are two safety rules to learn. By the end, you will be able to say both rules in your own words. You need your voice, and a grown-up nearby if one is there. No pencil needed! There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step one: Our first rule is this. If something on a screen makes you feel worried or upset, stop, close it, and tell a grown-up you trust. It is never your fault. Now you try. Tell me one grown-up you would go to. You can just say "my mum" or "my teacher" — no names needed.

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Welcome, Program Designer! Today we make a boat sail across the sea in ScratchJr. We do this because when we change the steps, we change what happens. By the end, you will build a program, guess what it does, and then run it to check. You need a tablet with ScratchJr open, and a pencil and paper for your guesses. A grown-up can sit with you. There are 6 small steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Open ScratchJr. Tap the house, then tap the plus sign to start a new project. I expect to see a big empty white space with blocks at the bottom. Tell me when your new project is open. 🚤

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today we are doing "Explain Your Thinking". This activity is not about circling an answer. It is about telling me WHY you think so, in your own words. We do this because a real designer can say why their program does what it does. By the end, you will be able to say your answer AND your reason out loud. You need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. Here is what I expect from you: a short answer, then the word "because", then your reason. Like this: "I choose the red car, because it is bigger."

There are 4 questions. Here comes question one. Two frogs are hopping. Frog A moves 2 steps. Frog B moves 8 steps. Which frog goes further? Tell me which one, and say "because..." 🐸

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Hello! Today you are a Program Designer. 🚤

This is our Unit Challenge: you will make a Boat sail across the sea in ScratchJr. First you build it, then you change one block and see what happens. We do this because it shows the big idea of our unit: when we change the steps, we change what happens. You will need a tablet with ScratchJr, and a grown-up nearby if you want help. There are 5 steps. I will give you one step at a time. Step 1: Open ScratchJr. Tap the plus sign to start a new project. Then pick a sea background. I expect to see: a new empty project with water on the screen. Tell me when your sea is ready!

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are starting Unit 5: We Can Network. A network is when we join two or more computers or devices together so they can talk and share. We are learning this because you use networks every day — a phone calling family far away is one! By the end you will be able to say what a network is, name devices that can join one, and tell me what the internet is. You need a pencil and a piece of paper. That is all. There are 5 small steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Hold up one finger for a tablet all by itself. Just one, nobody else. Now tell me: can that lonely tablet send a message to anyone? Say yes or no, and tell me why you think so. 😊

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for our lesson, "We Can Network". A network is when we join two or more computers or devices together. In this lesson you will learn what a network is, which things can join one, what a network lets us do, and what the internet is. By the end, you will be able to tell someone what a network is in your own words. You need a pencil, some paper, and your talking voice. There are 5 steps. Here is step 1. Imagine one tablet, all by itself. It is lonely. It cannot send a message to anybody, because nothing is joined to it. Now think about your home or your classroom. Can you name one device there? A phone, a tablet, a TV, a printer — anything like that. Tell me one device you can think of.

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Tools and Setup page for Unit 5, "We Can Network". Setup means getting ready before we learn. In this unit we will learn about networks — that is when we join two or more computers or devices together. The lovely thing is you do not need a computer for this unit! You just need a few simple things from home. What I expect from you: get each thing I ask for, then tell me "done" or "I can't find it". That's all. There are 4 steps. Step 1: Find a pencil and one sheet of paper. We will draw and circle things on it. Tell me when you have them. 😊

words.label: Computing Words
words.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Computing Words page. 📘

These are the six special words for Unit 5, We Can Network. We learn them so you can say what a network is, and talk about it like a real computer person. By the end, you will know each word and use it in your own sentence. You need your ears, your voice, and maybe a pencil. That's all! We have 6 steps — one word each. Here comes step one. Step 1: the word is network. A network is two or more computers or devices joined together. Say it with me, slowly: net-work. Now your turn. Tell me: how many devices do we need to make a network — one, or two or more?

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing "Can It Join a Network?"

A network is two or more devices joined together so they can talk and share. In this activity you will look at some things and decide which ones can join a network. By the end, you will be able to point at a thing and say yes or no. You need a pencil and a piece of paper (or your activity page). I expect you to try each one yourself first, tell me your answer, and say why. There are 4 steps. Step 1: Get your paper and pencil ready. Then write these seven words down the page, one under the other:
tablet, bicycle, phone, ball, printer, chair, laptop. Tell me when you have written them. Take your time — there's no rush.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. 🌟

A visual model is a picture that shows an idea. On this page there are five pictures, one for each big idea in "We Can Network". We look at each picture and say what it shows in our own words. That is how the idea sticks in your head. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are five steps, one picture each. I expect you to look carefully and tell me what you see, in your own words — even a few words is a great answer. Step 1: Find the first picture, called "What is a network?". Look at it for a moment. Then tell me: what do you see in that picture?

code.label: Code Examples
code.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Examples activity for Unit 5, We Can Network. In this unit we do not write code — we build networks with our hands and our words. So our examples are little networks that we draw. By the end you will be able to draw a network, name your devices, and say one thing a network lets us do. You need a piece of paper and a pencil. Your grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: On your paper, draw two devices. A device is a machine like a tablet, a phone or a printer. Draw any two you like — maybe a tablet and a phone. I expect two clear drawings, with a space between them. They do not have to be neat! Tell me when you have drawn them, and tell me which two you chose.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing "Learn the Method". A method is just a way of working, step by step. Ours is about networks. A network is two or more devices joined together so they can talk and share. By the end you will be able to say what a network is in your own words, and draw a tiny one. You need a pencil and a piece of paper. That's all! There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Say the big idea in your own words. Finish this sentence out loud, then type it to me: "A network is when we join ..."

A good answer says two or more devices, or computers, joined together. Take your time — there's no rush.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Worked Examples in Unit 5, We Can Network. Worked examples are little questions we solve together, one at a time. We do them so the big ideas of this unit stick in your head — network, device, share, internet. There are 6 examples. I will give you one at a time. Here is what I expect from you: try your own answer first, even if you are not sure. A guess is allowed! Then I will tell you what is good about it. You need your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. Ready? Here comes question one. Finish this sentence: A network is when we ______ two or more computers or devices together.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Quick Reference — it is like a little word box for Unit 5, We Can Network. We are doing this so the six special words of this unit stick in your head: network, connect, communicate, device, share, internet. By the end, you will be able to say each word and what it means, in your own words. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. Here is what I expect from you: say each word out loud, and try your own sentence — even a wobbly sentence is a great sentence. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Look at your Quick Reference page and find these three words: network, connect, communicate. Say each one out loud, slowly. Then tell me: which of those three words feels the hardest to you?

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice in Unit 5, "We Can Network". Guided Practice means we do five little questions together, one at a time. We do it so the big words stick in your head: network, device, internet. By the end, you will be able to say what a network is and name devices that can join one. You need your ears, your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. There are 5 steps, one question each. Here is what I expect from you: try your own answer first, even if you are not sure. A guess is a great start. I will help you if you get stuck. Here comes question one. A network is when we join two or more computers or devices ________. Can you finish that sentence for me?

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Hello! Today we are network builders. 🙂

In this activity you will make your very own network. A network means two or more devices joined together, like a tablet and a phone. We do this so you can see with your own eyes how devices join up and share. By the end, you will be able to point at your work and say "this is my network!"

You need playdough if you have it. No playdough? A pencil and paper works perfectly. There are 5 steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Get your things ready. Playdough, or a sheet of paper and a pencil. Tell me which one you have, and we will start.

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Debug It. 🐞

In Debug It, we hunt for muddles. A muddle is an idea that sounds right, but is a little bit wrong. I will show you one muddle at a time, and you tell me if it is right or wrong, and why. We do this because good computer people check ideas carefully. By the end, you will be able to spot a wrong idea about networks and fix it in your own words. What you need: just your voice or your typing. No pencil needed. What I expect: don't just say "wrong" — tell me the better idea too, in a full sentence. There are 5 muddles. Here comes the first one. Muddle 1: "A network is just one computer."

Is that right or wrong? And what would you say instead?

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are on the Games page of Unit 5, "We Can Network". These games are little quizzes that help the words stick in your head: network, connect, device, share, internet. We play them because remembering is easier when it feels like a game! By the end you will be able to say what a network is, and which things can join one. You need only your thinking brain, and a grown-up nearby if you want help reading. Here is what I expect from you: pick one answer each time, and tell me WHY you picked it. Guessing is fine — thinking out loud is better! We will play four rounds together. Here comes question one. True or false? A bicycle can join a network. Tell me true or false, and why. 🚲

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today we are doing Computing Fluency. Fluency means saying the answer quickly, without stopping to think hard. We do it so the network words stay strong in your head, like knowing your own name. By the end, you will be quick at five questions about networks. You just need your voice, and maybe a pencil. There are 5 questions, one at a time. Here is what I expect from you: try your best answer, even if you are not sure. A guess is fine! Mistakes are how we learn. Here comes question one. Finish this sentence: A network is when two or more computers or devices are ______ together.

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Stay Safe Online. This activity is about four rules that keep you safe when you use the internet. We do it because the internet joins us to people all over the world — that is lovely, but we must be careful too. By the end, you will be able to say the rules in your own words and know what to do if something feels wrong. You will need your ears, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. A grown-up nearby can help you. There are four rules, one for each step. Here comes step one. Rule 1: Keep personal information private. Personal information means things like your full name, your address, your school, your phone number and your passwords. We never type these into a game or a website, and never send them to someone we only know online. Your turn: tell me one thing that is personal information, and one thing that is NOT personal information. Take your time — there's no rush.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this activity is called Solve Real Problems. In it, you use what you know about networks to answer questions about real life — at home, at school, at the market, and in our community. We do this so the words network, device and internet become yours, not just words in a book. By the end you will be able to say what a network is and name devices that can join one. You need your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like. There are four questions, and I will give you one at a time. Here is question one. At home: True or false? A bicycle can join a network. I expect you to say true or false, and then tell me why in your own words. Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Explain Your Thinking."

In this activity you tell me the answer AND why you think it. That is the important part — the why. It helps the words from this unit stick in your head: network, connect, device, share, internet. You need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. There are 4 short thinking questions. I will give you one at a time. Here comes question one. Finish this sentence: "The internet is the biggest ______."

I expect one word to fill the gap, and then one little sentence telling me why. Take your time — there's no rush.

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Welcome to your Unit Project! Today you are a network builder. You are going to make two or more devices out of playdough, like a tablet, a phone or a printer. Then you will join them with playdough strings to make a network. We do this so you can show, with your own hands, what a network really is. By the end you will be able to point at your work and say: these devices are joined together, so they can share. What I expect from you: name each device you make, join them all up, and tell someone one thing you can do on the internet. You will need playdough (or paper and a pencil to draw it), and a grown-up nearby if you want help. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Think first, before you build. Tell me two or three devices you want to make. Pick ones that CAN join a network!

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Unit Challenge: We Can Network. You are going to build a real little network with your hands. You will make devices out of playdough, join them together, then tell someone about it. We do this so the word network stops being just a word — you will see it and touch it. You need playdough (or paper and a pencil, that works too), and a grown-up or a partner to show at the end. There are 4 steps. Here is Step 1. Make two or more devices out of playdough. A device is a machine like a tablet, a phone or a printer. A good tablet is a flat square. A good phone is a small flat rectangle. Make at least two. Tell me when your devices are made, and tell me which ones you made. 😊

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Welcome to Unit 6! I am your teacher today. This unit is called "Be a Problem Solver". It is about putting steps in the right order, and finding mistakes and fixing them. We do this because computers only work when our steps are in the right order. By the end, you will be able to order steps, spot a wrong step, and fix a mistake in a program. You need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain! We have 4 small steps on this Overview page. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look at the unit title on your screen: "Be a Problem Solver". Now tell me — what do you think a problem solver does? Any answer is welcome. I am listening. 😊

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and our job is to get our tool ready. Our tool is called ScratchJr. It is a free app where you drag coloured picture blocks to make a character move. We set it up now so that later we can make a character walk to the park. Here is what I expect from you: get a tablet with a grown-up's help, follow one small step at a time, and tell me when each step is done. There are 4 steps. No reading is needed in the app, and you do not make an account. Step 1: Open the ScratchJr app on your tablet. Tell me when you see it open. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the lesson called Be a Problem Solver. In this lesson we learn how to put steps in the right order, and how to find a mistake and fix it. We do this because a computer only works if we tell it things in the right order. By the end, you will know two new words: algorithm and bug. You need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking voice. There are 4 steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1. Think about making anjero. Here are the steps, all mixed up:
cook the anjero
mix the flour and water
eat the yummy anjero
pour the batter on the hot pan

Tell me just one thing: which step do we do FIRST? I expect one short answer, in your own words.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing "Put the Anjero in Order". In this activity you take four steps for making anjero and put them in the right order. We do this because steps only work in the right order — you cannot cook the anjero before you mix it! By the end, you will be able to make an algorithm, which is just a list of steps in the right order. You need a pencil and your activity page (or a piece of paper). There are 4 steps in our activity. I expect you to think first, then tell me your answer — no rushing. Here comes step one. Look at the four mixed-up cards:
Cook the anjero
Mix the flour and water
Eat the yummy anjero
Pour the batter on the hot pan

Tell me just this: which one do we do FIRST?

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Welcome to Computing Words! This page holds the special words we use in Unit 6, Be a Problem Solver. We learn these words so you can talk like a real problem solver — and so the rest of the unit makes sense when you meet the words again. By the end you will know three big words and be able to use them in your own sentences. You need your ears, your voice, and maybe a pencil. There are 4 steps. Ready? Step 1. Say this word with me, slowly: step. A step means one thing you do. Mixing the flour is one step. Putting on your shoe is one step. Now you try: tell me one step you did this morning. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Visual Models. Visual Models are little picture-cards. Each one shows one big idea from our unit, Be a Problem Solver. We look at each card and say what it means in our own words. That helps the idea stick in your head. You will need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil. There are five cards, so we will do five small steps. One at a time — take your time, there's no rush. Step 1: Look at the first card. It is called "Steps in the right order". Look at the picture and the words, then tell me one thing you notice. What do you notice? 🙂

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are on Learn the Method. A method is a way of working. Ours is called "steps in the right order." We will use the anjero steps — mix, pour, cook, eat — to practise it. By the end, you will be able to put steps in the right order and say why the order matters. You need your ears, your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Tell me in your own words what an algorithm is. A good answer says something like "a list of steps in the right order." Say it your way — I am listening.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing Worked Examples. A worked example is a puzzle with the answer shown, so you can see HOW a problem solver thinks. We do this so that when you get a puzzle on your own, you know what to do. By the end, you will be able to put steps in order and spot a wrong step. You need a pencil and paper, and your thinking brain! We have 3 short steps. Here comes step one. We are making anjero. Here are three steps, all mixed up:
Cook
Mix
Pour

On your paper, write these three words in the right order. Which one do you do first? Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me when you are done!

code.label: Code Examples
code.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is our Code Examples page. Code just means the picture blocks we join together in ScratchJr. On this page we read a program like a little story: what starts it, and what happens next. We do this so that later you can spot a bug — a mistake in a program — and fix it all by yourself. What I expect from you: look carefully, say your answer out loud or type it, and guess bravely. A wrong guess is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step one: Look at the top block of the program. In ScratchJr, every program starts with a yellow block at the top. Point to the top block with your finger. Tell me: what does the yellow top block have on it — a green flag, or a hand tapping?

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice in Unit 6, Be a Problem Solver. In this activity we practise three things: putting steps in the right order, finding a wrong step, and spotting a bug. We do it because computers follow our steps exactly — so the order has to be right. By the end, you will be able to fix a mistake all by yourself. You need a pencil and paper, and your thinking brain! What I expect from you: try each one first, then tell me your answer. Mistakes are how we learn, so don't worry. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Making anjero. Here are the steps, all mixed up:

Cook the anjero
Mix the flour and water
Eat the yummy anjero
Pour the batter on the hot pan

Write 1, 2, 3, 4 next to them. Tell me your order when you are ready. Take your time — there's no rush.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Computing Words page — it holds all the important words from Unit 6, Be a Problem Solver. We are doing this so the words feel easy in your mouth, not hard. By the end you will be able to say three words and use each one in your own sentence.
