You need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. Here is what I expect from you: try each word out loud, then make your own sentence about your own life — your food, your school, your toys. A short sentence is perfect. We have 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1. Our first word is step. A step means one thing you do. When we make anjero, mixing the flour is one step. Now say it with me, slowly: step... one thing you do. Now make your own sentence with it. Tell me one step you do in the morning.

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Welcome to Build It! Today you are the maker. 🌟

In this activity we help Leo walk to the park. First we plan the steps, then we build them in ScratchJr with the picture blocks, then we tap the green flag to see if it works. We do this because a computer only does what our blocks say. Putting steps in the right order is called an algorithm — a list of steps in the right order. What I expect from you: try each step yourself, tell me when it is done, and tell me what you see on the screen. If Leo goes the wrong way, that is fine! That is a bug, and we will fix it together. You need a tablet with ScratchJr open, and your paper with Leo's steps if you have it. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Open ScratchJr. Tap the big plus to start a new project. Then tell me when your empty white stage is showing.

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and our activity is called Debug It. A bug is a mistake in a program. Debugging means we find the mistake and fix it. We do this because computers do exactly what we say, not what we mean — so when something goes wrong, WE are the ones who fix it. By the end, you will be able to find one wrong step and say what it should be. You need a pencil and paper, and your thinking brain. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Look at these steps for the star. We WANT the star to move 2 steps UP. Step 1: Move 2 steps up
Step 2: Move 2 steps down

One of these is wrong. Write down the number of the wrong step on your paper, and tell me which one it is. I expect just one number, and if you can, tell me why. Take your time — there's no rush.

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Computing Fluency. Fluency means quick practice. I ask you a short question, you answer, and we check it together. It helps the important words stay in your head — words like step, order, bug and debug. By the end you will answer quickly and feel sure about them. You need: your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are 4 questions. Here comes question one. In ScratchJr, which block starts the program when you tap the green flag? Is it Start on Tap, or Start on Green Flag?

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to the Games page! These little games are practice for Unit 6 — being a problem solver. Each game gives you four short questions about steps, order, algorithms and bugs. We play them so the words stick in your head and feel easy. All you need is your finger to tap, and your brain to think first! Here is what I expect from you: think about your answer BEFORE you tap, and tell me what you picked and why. Even one word for "why" is great. There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Look at the games on your screen. Tap the first one, called "Quick Match: step". Then tell me when it has opened. 🙂

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Hello! Today we are learning how to stay safe online. This is our Stay Safe Online page. It has three safety rules for using the internet. We do this so you know what to do when you are on a tablet or computer. By the end, you will be able to say each rule in your own words. You just need your eyes, your ears, and your talking voice. A grown-up nearby can help too. There are three steps, one rule each time. Step 1: Read this rule with me. "Check before you trust." Anyone can put anything on the internet. So not everything you read is true. Now tell me: if you see something online, who is a good person to ask about it?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Solve Real Problems. In this activity you use what you learned about steps, order and bugs — but on real little problems, like a real problem solver. By the end you will be able to spot a wrong step and say how to fix it. You need a pencil and paper, and your thinking brain. That is all! There are 4 problems. I will give you one at a time, and I will wait for you. Here comes question one. We want the Moon to go UP. But the step says: Move 2 steps down. Is that step right or wrong? Tell me what you think. 🌙

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Welcome to your Unit 6 Project — you are going to be a problem solver! Here is what we will do. You will help Leo walk to the park. First you plan the steps on paper, then you build it in ScratchJr, then you find and fix a bug. We do this because computers only do what we tell them. Planning first makes it work, and fixing mistakes makes you a real problem solver. What I expect from you: try each step, tell me what happened, and stay happy even if it goes wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. You need a pencil, paper, and a tablet with ScratchJr. There are 5 steps. Step 1: On your paper, draw a small map. Put an L in one corner for Leo. Put a P in another corner for the park. Draw squares in between, like a little path. Tell me when your map is drawn! 🗺️

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and our activity is the Unit 6 Challenge: Be a Problem Solver. Here is what we will do. We will help Leo walk to the park. First you plan the steps on paper. Then you build them in ScratchJr. Then, if something goes wrong, you find the mistake and fix it. A mistake in a program is called a bug, and fixing it is called debugging. By the end you will be able to plan a list of steps, run it, and fix a bug all by yourself. You will need a pencil and paper, and a tablet with ScratchJr. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 5 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Draw your map on paper. Draw a small grid of squares, like a window with 9 or 12 boxes. Put the letter L in one corner for Leo. Put the letter P in a different corner for the park. I am looking for one L, one P, and squares you can count with your finger. Tell me when your map is drawn. 🙂

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Welcome! Today we are doing Explain Your Thinking. That means you tell me your answer AND why. Talking out your thinking is how a problem solver works. By the end, you will be able to explain the order of steps in your own words. You just need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. Here is what I expect: short answers are fine, but always add a "because". For example, "I put mix first because..."

There are 4 short questions. Here comes question one. We are making anjero. Here are three steps:
Mix
Pour
Cook

Which one is number 1? Tell me why. 😊

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today we start Unit 7. It is called Computers Control Things. Here is the big idea. Tiny computers hide inside everyday things, and they are the boss. This page is our map for the whole unit — we look at it first so you know where we are going. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil. What I expect from you is easy: think, then tell me your answer in your own words. Guessing is allowed. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Look around your home in your mind. Think of ONE machine that does a clever job — like a washing machine, a microwave, or a toy that makes a sound. Tell me the one you picked.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Today's lesson is called "Computers Control Things". We are doing it to find a secret: tiny computers hide inside many things at home! By the end, you will be able to spot them, know what a robot is, and name how a computer talks back to us. You just need your eyes, your voice, and a pencil if you like. There are 5 small steps. Here comes step 1. Look around your home in your mind. Think of the washing machine. It has a tiny computer hiding inside! We cannot see it, but it is the boss. It tells the machine what to do. That is called control. Your turn: tell me one machine in your home that you think has a hidden computer inside. A good answer names one thing, like "the microwave".

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! I'm your teacher today, and this page is called Tools and Setup. Setup means getting ready before we start. In this unit, Computers Control Things, we will hunt for hidden computers, meet robots, and build our very own robot from boxes. So first we gather what we need. Here is what I expect from you: gather each thing, then tell me "done" so I can check. Ask a grown-up to help when you need to reach or cut. There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Find a pencil and some paper. Colours too, if you have them. That's all you need for the first activities. Tell me when you have them. 🙂

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Welcome to our Computing Words lesson! Today we learn the special words of Unit 7, "Computers Control Things". Knowing these words helps you talk like a real computer scientist. We will do this in three steps, and I will give you one step at a time. Here is what I expect from you: say each word out loud, tell me what it means in your own words, then make your very own sentence with it. Your own words are best — not copying mine. You will need your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like writing. Step 1. Our first word is computer. A computer is a clever machine that follows steps and can control other things. A tablet is a computer. A laptop is a computer. Now you try: tell me one computer you have seen at home or at school. 😊

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Explore the Concept. In this activity we find out something surprising. Tiny computers hide inside everyday things, and they are the boss. By the end you will be able to spot them, and say what a robot is. All you need is your eyes, your thinking, and maybe a pencil. There are 5 small steps. Here comes step one. Step one: think about your kitchen at home. Tell me one machine you see there. It could be a fridge, a microwave, or a washing machine. I expect just one word or a short sentence from you. Take your time — there's no rush.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing Visual Models. A visual model is just a picture that helps an idea stick in your head. We have five little picture-ideas in this unit, all about how computers control things. By the end, you will be able to tell me what each picture means in your own words. You need a pencil and some paper. That is all! There are five steps, one for each picture. Here comes step one. Step 1: Picture in your head a washing machine. Now draw a little box inside it, hiding. That box is the tiny computer. Under your drawing, tell me one thing you think that hidden computer tells the washing machine to do. I am hoping for something like "it tells it when to stop" — any sensible job is great. Take your time — there's no rush. 😊

code.label: Code Examples
code.text:
Hello! I'm Wehel Tutor, and I'm your teacher for this activity today. This page is called Code Examples. In Grade 1 we do not type code yet. Instead we read the STEPS that a hidden computer follows inside a machine. We do this because a computer is not clever like you — it only follows the steps people give it. By the end you will be able to say what a hidden computer controls, and what it tells us back. You need a pencil and paper, or just your voice. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Think of one machine in your home that has a tiny computer hiding inside it. A microwave, a washing machine, or a fridge are all good ones. Tell me which one you pick, and say one thing its computer controls. A good answer sounds like this: "A fridge. Its computer keeps our food cold."

Take your time — there's no rush.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice. In this activity we practise the big idea of Unit 7: computers hide inside things, and they control them. We do it so the ideas stick in your head, like a song you know by heart. By the end, you will be able to spot a computer inside everyday things and name output devices. All you need is your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are 5 questions. I will give you one at a time, and I will wait for you. Take your time — there's no rush. Here comes question one. Look at these four things: tablet, ball, washing machine, spoon. Which ones have a computer hiding inside them? You can tell me one, or both. A good answer names the thing and says "it has a computer inside".

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Quick Reference page. This page is our word box for Unit 7. It holds the important words: computer, device, control, output, robot and android. We go through it so the words stick in your head, and so you can use them when you talk about machines at home. By the end, you will be able to say each word and give your own example. You need your ears, your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are 5 steps. Ready? Step 1. Let's start with the word control. Control means to tell something what to do. Here is my example: the computer inside a washing machine controls it — it tells the machine how long to wash. Now your turn. Say the word control out loud, then tell me in your own words what control means. A good answer uses words like "tell it what to do".

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a question with the thinking shown, so we learn how to answer it. We will do a few of these together about computers that hide inside things, robots, and output. By the end, you will be able to say which things have a computer inside, and what a robot is. You need a pencil and a piece of paper. Take your time — there's no rush. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Look at these four things: a tablet, a ball, a washing machine, a spoon. Write down the ones you think have a computer hiding inside. A good answer picks the clever things that follow steps — not the plain, simple things. Tell me your list when you are ready. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! I'm Wehel Tutor, and today I'm your teacher. 😊

This page is called Learn the Method. A method is just a way of doing something, step by step. Today's method helps us find the hidden computers inside everyday things and say what each one does. By the end, you will be able to pick any machine at home and tell me the computer inside it and its job. You need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking voice. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Say the big idea in your own words. The big idea is this — lots of everyday things have a tiny computer hiding inside, and that computer controls the thing. Control means it tells the thing what to do. Now you say it back to me in your own words. It does not have to be perfect. A good answer uses the word control or "tells it what to do."

Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Welcome to Build It! Today you are going to make your very own robot. A robot is a machine that does a job by itself. It has a tiny computer inside, and that computer controls it — it tells it what to do. By the end, you will have a robot you planned, built and named, and you will be able to tell someone its job and its output. You will need paper, a pencil, colours, and some cardboard boxes, tubes or bottle caps. Ask your grown-up to help you find those. There are 5 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Think of a job for your robot. What one job will it do all by itself? Maybe it cleans the floor, waters the plants, or helps in the kitchen. I expect one clear job, said in a full sentence like this: "My robot's job is to ______."

Tell me your robot's job when you have it. Take your time — there's no rush.

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Welcome to Debug It! Here is what we are doing today. A "bug" is a mistake in an idea. On this page there are wrong ideas about computers and robots, and your job is to be the detective who fixes them. This helps you really understand what a computer does and what a robot is. All you need is your thinking, and a pencil if you like. There are six bugs. I will give you one at a time. Here is what I expect from you: for each bug, tell me if it is true or not true, and say why in your own words. A good answer has two parts — "no, that's wrong" and "because...". Bug number one:
"A computer is only a laptop or a tablet."

Is that true? Tell me what you think. 🕵️

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today we are playing the Unit 7 games. A game here is just a fun quiz — I say a question, you pick or say your answer. We do this to make our new words stick: computer, control, robot, output. By the end, you will be able to say what hides inside a washing machine, and what a robot really is. You need nothing but your thinking brain. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 4 rounds. Here comes question one. Which one of these has a tiny computer hiding inside it — a spoon, or a washing machine?

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Computing Fluency. Fluency means quick and sure — like knowing your own name. We do it so the big ideas of Unit 7 come to you fast, without hard thinking. There are 5 short questions. I will give you one at a time. Here is what I expect from you: answer in a full sentence, in your own words. Say why, not just yes or no. It is fine to be wrong — mistakes are how we learn. You need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. Ready? Here comes question one. Which of these have a computer hiding inside them? A tablet, a ball, a washing machine, a spoon.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! Today we are doing "Solve Real Problems" together. In this activity, you use what you learned about computers and robots to answer real-life questions. Not just remembering words — thinking! By the end, you will be able to look at a thing and say if a computer is hiding inside it. There are 4 questions. You need your voice, or a pencil and paper. And your thinking brain! 🙂

What I expect from you: try to answer in a full sentence, not just one word. It is fine to be wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. Here comes question one. At home, your family has a robot that looks like a person. It has a face, arms and legs. What do we call a robot that looks like a person? Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Welcome to Explain Your Thinking! In this activity you tell me your answer in your own words, not just one word. It helps you really understand computers, not just remember them. By the end, you will be able to explain what a computer inside a machine does. You just need your voice, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are 4 short questions. Take your time — there's no rush. Here comes question one. A computer hides inside a washing machine. What do you think that computer does? Tell me in a full sentence, like this shape: "The computer... "

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Welcome to Stay Safe Online! On this page we learn three rules that keep us safe when we use a computer or a tablet. We do this because computers are fun, but we need to be smart and safe too. By the end, you will be able to say all three rules in your own words. All you need is you and your thinking brain! There are three steps, one rule each. Step 1. Here is our first rule: Check before you trust. Anyone can put anything on the internet. So not everything you read is true! If something looks important, check it on another website too, and ask a grown-up if you are not sure. Now your turn: tell me in your own words why we should not believe everything on the internet. Just one sentence is perfect. 😊

project.label: Unit Project
project.text:
Welcome to your Unit 7 Project! Today you are going to design and build your very own robot. Here is why we do it. In this unit you learned that a robot is a machine with a computer inside, and it does a job all by itself. Making your own robot helps you show that you really understand it. By the end you will have a robot with a name, a job, and an output — and you will be able to tell someone all about it. What you need: a pencil, some paper, and later some boxes, tubes and bottle caps. A grown-up can help you find those. What I expect from you: one clear job for your robot, a robot you built with your hands, one output you chose, and then you tell someone about it. That's four things. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Step one: think of ONE job for your robot. Not two jobs — just one. Maybe it waters the plants. Maybe it picks up toys. Write it down like this: "My robot's job is ______."

Take your time — there's no rush. Tell me the job when you have it! 🤖

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Unit Challenge: you are going to design and build your very own robot. We do this because a robot is a machine with a computer inside that does a job all by itself. When you give your robot a job, you are being the boss — just like people are the boss of every computer. By the end you will have a robot you made, with a name, a job, and an output. You will need paper, a pencil, colours, and some empty boxes or tubes. Ask your grown-up to help you find those. There are five steps. I will give you one at a time. 🙂

Step 1: Choose your robot's job. Think of ONE job your robot does all by itself. Maybe it cleans the floor, or waters the plants, or feeds the cat. What I expect: one clear job, said in a full sentence, like "My robot's job is to ______."

Tell me your robot's job when you are ready. Take your time — there's no rush.

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! I am your teacher today, and this is our Tools and Setup page for Unit 8, Be a Data Collector. In this unit you will ask people questions and write down their answers. That is called collecting data. Good news — you do not need a computer for this unit. You just need a few simple things, and today we get them ready. Here is what I expect from you: get each thing, then tell me "done". If you cannot find something, tell me and we will pick another one together. There are 4 steps. Step 1: Find a pencil. A pencil is best, because a data collector sometimes needs to rub something out. Go and get one now, and tell me when you have it. You can ask your grown-up to help you look. 😊

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Welcome to Unit 8: Be a Data Collector! 🍋

Here is what this page is. It is our first look at the whole unit. We find out what we will learn, and we meet the new words. That way, nothing feels strange later. By the end of this unit you will ask a question, write down the answers, and make a colour chart from them. Just like a real data collector! What I expect from you today: answer me in your own words, even if it is just a few words. You do not need anything except your thinking. A pencil and paper is nice to have. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Tell me what you already know about this. What do you think a data collector does?

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Welcome to Unit 8, my data collector! 🎉

Here is what we are doing today. In this lesson you will learn how to find things out, write them down, and turn them into a picture chart. That picture chart tells you which thing is the favourite. By the end you will be able to say what data is, use tally marks, and read a pictogram. What you need: a pencil, a piece of paper, and some colours. What I expect from you: you answer with your own words, and you try each step even if it feels wobbly. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: What is data? Data is the little bits of what we find out. Your favourite fruit is data. The number of children in your class is data. Now you tell me: what is your favourite fruit — mango, banana, or dates? 🥭🍌

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Welcome to our Computing Words page! These are the special words for Unit 8, "Be a Data Collector". We do this so the words feel easy when you use them later — when you ask your friends questions and make your chart. By the end, you will know what each word means, and you will make your own sentence with one of them. All you need is your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. We have three steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Let's learn three new words together. data — the little bits of what we find out. Like: Nadia likes mango. collect — to find things out and gather them. record — to write it down so we do not forget. Now say them back to me in your own words. Just tell me what "data" means. I am listening!

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Visual Models page. A visual model is a picture that shows an idea. On this page there are five little picture cards, one for each big idea in our unit: what data is, using a form, sorting and tallying, making a pictogram, and being a data collector. We do this so the ideas stick in your head as pictures, not just words. By the end, you will be able to say each idea in your own words. You need a pencil, some paper, and your voice. That is all. There are five steps — one for each picture card. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look at the first card, "What is data?" Read it, then tell me in your own words: what does a data collector do? I am hoping for a short answer like "they ask, then they write it down." Take your time — there's no rush.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are going to be data collectors. Data means the little bits of what we find out. Like your favourite fruit! A data collector asks a question, listens, and writes the answer down. By the end you will collect answers, count them with little marks, and colour a picture chart called a pictogram. You need a pencil and a sheet of paper (or the activity page). There are six small steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Tick your favourite fruit. On your paper, write these three words, one under the other, with a little box next to each:
Mango
Banana
Dates

Now tick ONE box — the fruit you like best. I expect one tick only, next to one fruit. That tick is your data! Tell me when it is done, and which one you ticked. 🙂

code.label: Code Examples
code.text:
Welcome! Today we are looking at the example on your screen. It shows tally marks — little lines we make, one line for each person who answers. We do this so you can read someone else's data and turn it into numbers. By the end, you will be able to count tally marks and say how many, which fruit is the most, and which is the fewest. You need a pencil, a piece of paper, and your counting voice. There are 4 small steps. Here comes step one. Look at the mango row on the screen:
Mango | | | | |

Point at each little line with your finger and count out loud, one line at a time. Then tell me the number you get. I am expecting one number from you — and you should touch each line once as you count, so no line gets counted twice. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a small question with the answer shown, so we can see how a data collector thinks. We are doing this to get ready to collect real data ourselves — asking, writing it down, and counting. By the end, you will be able to say what a data collector does, and read a picture chart to find the favourite. You need a pencil and a piece of paper. There are six little examples. We will do one at a time. Here comes number one. A data collector asks a question, listens, and writes it down. So tell me: what does a data collector do? Say it in your own words. 😊

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are on the Learn the Method page. Here is what this page is. A method is just the way we do a job, step by step. Our job is being a data collector: ask a question, write down the answers, count them, and show them in a picture chart. We do this so you can find things out and show them to other people. By the end you will be able to say the method in your own words, and try it with a small example. You will need a pencil and a piece of paper. That is all! There are 4 steps. Here is step one. Step 1: Tell me the main idea in your own words. I ask you: what does a data collector do? Say it your own way — one short sentence is perfect. A good answer says something about finding things out and writing them down. Off you go — I am listening. 🙂

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Guided Practice. In this activity we practise being a data collector. A data collector asks a question, listens, and writes the answers down. We will do six short questions together. By the end, you will be able to read a picture chart and say which one is the most. You need a pencil and some paper. That is all! I expect you to try each one yourself first. A good answer is a full sentence, not just one word. If you get stuck, say "stuck" and I will give you a small hint. Mistakes are how we learn. Here comes question one. What does a data collector do?

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Welcome! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Quick Reference — it is like a little word box for Unit 8, Be a Data Collector. We are doing this so the big words stop feeling big. When you know the words, the pictograms and tally marks become easy. By the end you will be able to say what data, tally and pictogram mean, in your own words. You need a pencil and paper, and your voice. There are 4 steps, one at a time. Step 1. Our first word is data. Data means the little bits of what we find out. Your favourite fruit is data. The number of shoes by your door is data. Here is what I expect from you: tell me one bit of data about YOU. It can be your favourite colour, or your favourite food. One short sentence is perfect. 🙂

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are going to be data collectors. 🧺

Here is what that means. Data is the little bits we find out — like which fruit someone likes best. A data collector asks a question, writes the answers down, and then makes a picture chart called a pictogram. We do this so we can look at our chart and see the answer straight away: which fruit is the favourite. What you need: a piece of paper, a pencil, and some colours. A grown-up or a few family members nearby to ask. There are 5 steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1: On your paper, write three words down the left side, one under the other: Mango, Banana, Dates. Leave lots of space next to each word — that is where your marks will go. I expect three neat words, one below the other, with space beside them. Tell me when it is done!

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Welcome to Debug It! 🕵️

In this activity we look at little mix-ups about being a data collector. A mix-up is a wrong idea. Our job is to spot it and fix it, like a detective. This helps you remember the right way when you make your own tally and pictogram. You need a pencil and paper, and your thinking brain. There are six mix-ups. I will give you one at a time, and you tell me what is wrong with it. A good answer says "that is wrong because..." in your own words. Do not worry about getting it perfect — mistakes are how we learn. Here comes mix-up one. Someone says: "Data is a hard word. Only computers have data."

Do you think that is right or wrong? Tell me why.

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Computing Fluency. Fluency means quick practice. We say the important ideas from Unit 8 again and again, until they come out fast and easy. By the end, you will know what a data collector does, what a form is, and how to read a pictogram. You need: your eyes, your voice, and maybe a pencil. That's all! Here is what I expect from you. Try each answer by yourself first. Answer in a full sentence if you can. If you are stuck, say "stuck" and I will give you a small hint — never the answer straight away. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 7 questions, in two rounds. Ready? Here comes question one. What does a data collector do? 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are going to play the Unit 8 games. A game here is just practice. It asks you a question about being a data collector, and you pick the answer you think is right. We play so the important words — data, tally, pictogram — stay in your head nice and strong. By the end, you will be able to say what data is and how a pictogram works, all by yourself. You need only your eyes, your thinking brain, and the game on your screen. There are four little rounds in one game. I will take you through them one at a time. Here comes step one. Look at your screen and find the first game. It is called Quick Match: data. Click it to start, and read the first question slowly to yourself. What I expect from you: don't rush, and don't press an answer yet. Just tell me here what the first question is asking. Take your time — there's no rush.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! Let's be data detectives at home, school and the market today. This page is called Solve Real Problems. That means we use our data skills in real places, not just on a worksheet. You will look at some data, then work out which thing is the most and which is the fewest. By the end you will be able to read a chart and answer questions about it, all by yourself. You need a pencil and paper, and your counting fingers. 😊

There are four steps — one for home, one for school, one for the market, one for our community. Here comes step one. At home, Mum wrote down the fruit her family ate this week:

Mango: | | | | |
Banana: | | |
Dates: | |

Those little lines are tally marks. One mark means one fruit. Count the marks for mango and tell me the number. Take your time — there's no rush.

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text:
Welcome to our Stay Safe Online page! 🌟

This is our safety part of Unit 8. We are data collectors — we find things out and write them down. Some of that data lives on computers and on the internet. So we need to know how to stay safe there. By the end you will know three safety rules, and you will be able to say each one in your own words. You just need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. There are three steps — one rule for each step. Step 1: Our first rule is "Check before you trust."
Anyone can put anything on the internet. So not everything you read is true! If something is important, look it up in a second place too, and ask a grown-up you trust. Now you try: tell me in your own words what "check before you trust" means. Even one short sentence is perfect.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher for this one. 😊

This page is called Explain Your Thinking. That means you tell me your answer AND why you think it. Not just one word — your own words. We do this because a real data collector can say what their chart shows. That is a big skill! There are four short questions. For each one I want a full sentence, using our unit words like data, form, tally and pictogram. There are no silly answers here — your thinking is what counts. You need nothing but your brain and maybe a pencil. Here comes question one. A form is a list of questions we fill in. Some forms are on paper, and some are on a computer. Tell me: what is a computer form? Say it in your own words.

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Welcome to your Unit Project! Today you become a real data collector. You will ask a few friends one question: what is your favourite fruit — mango, banana, or dates? You will write down every answer with a tally mark, count the marks, colour a pictogram, and find the favourite fruit. We do this so you can see how data turns into a picture we can read. You need a pencil, some paper, and colours. If you like, ask your grown-up to help you find people to ask. What I expect from you: a real answer from each person, one tally mark for each answer, and a pictogram where one box means one person. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: On your paper, write three rows — Mango, Banana, Dates. Leave space next to each word for your marks. Tell me when your paper is ready. 🍌

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text: Welcome to your Unit Challenge! This is the big one — you become a real data collector. Here is what it is. You will ask a few friends or family one question: what is your favourite fruit — mango, banana, or dates? You will write down every answer, count them, colour a chart, and find the winner fruit. Why we do it: this is how real people find things out. Ask, record, count, look. What you need: a piece of paper, a pencil, and some colours. What I expect from you: one tally mark for every single answer, neat counting, and a chart that matches your marks. There are 5 steps. Ready? Here comes step one. Step 1: Get your paper. Write three words down the left side, one under the other: Mango, Banana, Dates. Leave lots of space next to each word for your marks. Tell me when your paper is ready. 🍋

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Tools and Setup page. This is where we get our tool ready. Our tool is ScratchJr — a free app where you join picture blocks to make a game. By the end you will have the app open and a brand new empty project, ready for your frog game. You need a tablet, and a grown-up nearby to help you open the app. Here is what I expect from you: try each step, then tell me "done" or "I'm stuck". There are 4 small steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Find the ScratchJr app on your tablet and tap it to open it. Look for a little face with an orange background. Tell me when it is open. 🐸

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Welcome to Unit 9! This unit is called Be a Games Developer. A games developer is a person who makes computer games — and that is you now. On this page we look at what we will learn before we start making. By the end of this little tour, you will know our three star words and the app we will use. All you need is your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. 🙂

There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Think about a game you have played on a tablet or a phone. Tell me one thing you did in it. Did you tap the screen? Did you make something jump or run? A good answer is just one short sentence, like "I tapped a bird to make it fly."

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and our lesson is called Be a Games Developer. A games developer is a person who makes computer games. In this lesson you will learn to make a tiny game, try it, and fix it when it goes wrong. By the end, you will know three big words: testing, error, and debug. You need a pencil, some paper, and your thinking brain. A tablet with ScratchJr is lovely too, but you can do a lot on paper. There are 5 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Think about a game you have played on a tablet or a phone. What did you do — tap the screen? Make something jump? Tell me one game you like, and one thing you do in it. That is all I need from you right now. 🐸

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Welcome to Computing Words! This page holds the special words for Unit 9, Be a Games Developer. We learn these words so that when we make our own games, we can say exactly what we are doing — like a real games developer. By the end, you will know what each word means and be able to use it in your own sentence. You need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. There are 7 words, so we will do them in small groups: 3 words, then 3 words, then 1 last one. What I expect from you: say the word out loud, then tell me its meaning in YOUR own words — not copied from the page. Then make one sentence of your own with it. Step 1 of 7. Our first word is games developer. It means a person who makes computer games. Say it with me, slowly: games de-vel-op-er. Now tell me — in your own words, who is a games developer?

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Visual Models. A visual model is a picture that shows one big idea. This page has five pictures, one for each idea in our games unit. We look at each one and say what it means in our own words. By the end, you will know all five ideas: games developer, testing, error, debug, and making your own game. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. There are five steps — one picture each time. Step 1. Look at the first model: "We are games developers!"

Tell me in your own words: what do you think a games developer is? Just have a guess. 🐸

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are being games developers. A games developer is a person who makes computer games. In this activity you will make a tiny tap game — you tap your character, and it hops! Why we do it: so you learn the magic habit. Make it, then try it. Trying your program to see if it works is called testing. What I expect from you: pick your own character, put the blocks in the right order, tap to test, and stay happy when something goes wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. You will need a tablet with ScratchJr if you have one, and paper and a pencil. A grown-up can help you open the app. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one! Step 1: Choose your character. Your character is the thing in your game. Pick one: frog, cat, dog, or bird. Then tell me what you want it to do when you tap it — hop, move, or say a word. Tell me your two choices, and we will go to step 2. 🐸

code.label: Code Examples
code.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher today, and this is our Code Examples activity. In ScratchJr, code is made of picture blocks. Blocks are little pieces that tell your character what to do. We look at code examples so you can read the blocks before you build them — just like reading a recipe before you cook. By the end you will be able to read a tiny block program, say what it does, and spot a block that is wrong. What I expect from you: read each block carefully, answer in your own words, and it is fine to guess. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Here is our code example. Three blocks, joined together:

Start on Tap
Hop 4
End

Look at the middle block. Tell me: what do you think the frog will do?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are learning the Method — the way a real games developer works. 🐸

It is four little steps: say the idea, copy the example, change one thing and guess what happens, then run it and see. We do this so your game does what YOU wanted, not something silly. What I expect from you: try each step, tell me when it is done, and tell me what you see — even if it goes wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. You need a tablet with ScratchJr if you have one. If not, paper and a pencil work fine. Step 1 of 4. Tell me the big idea in your own words: what does testing mean?

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a puzzle with the answer shown, so we can see HOW to think. We are doing this so you can be a games developer — someone who makes computer games. By the end you will know three big words: testing, error, and debug. Here is what I expect from you: try each one yourself first, in your own words. Short answers are fine. Wrong answers are fine too — mistakes are how we learn. There are six little examples. We go one at a time. Here comes question one. What does testing mean? Tell me in your own words. Here is a clue: it is something we do AFTER we make our game.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing Guided Practice for Unit 9, Be a Games Developer. Guided Practice means we answer some little questions together about making games. We do it so the game words stay in your head: testing, error, and debug. By the end you will be able to say what testing means and spot a wrong block. You need your listening ears, and a pencil if you like to write. What I expect: you try each answer yourself, even if you are not sure. A wrong try is fine — mistakes are how we learn. There are 6 small questions. Here comes question one. What does testing mean? Is it trying your program to see if it works, or is it eating your lunch? 🐸

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Computing Words card for Unit 9. It holds the special words a games developer uses. We learn them so you can say what you did with your game, in the right words. By the end, you will know three big words and use each one in your own sentence. You need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: our first word is testing. Testing means trying your program to see if it works. Like tapping the frog to see if it hops. Now you try: tell me one thing at home you test to see if it works. 🐸

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Hello! Today you are a games developer — a person who makes computer games. 🐸

In this activity you will build your very own tap game in ScratchJr. Your character will do something fun when you tap it. Then you will test it — that means you try it to see if it works. By the end, you will have a game you made yourself, and you will know how to test it. What you need: a tablet with ScratchJr open, and your grown-up nearby if you need help. What I expect from you: try each step, then tell me what happened — even if it goes wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Open ScratchJr. Tap the big plus sign to start a new project. Tell me when your new empty page is ready.

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello! I'm Wehel Tutor, and today I'm your teacher for Debug It. 🐸

Here is what this activity is. When a game does the wrong thing, that is an error. Finding the mistake and fixing it is called debugging. Today you will be the bug detective: you will look at some blocks, find the one block that is wrong, and say what it should be. Why we do it? Because every games developer does this all day. Even the grown-ups who make your favourite games find bugs and fix them. Mistakes are normal! You need your page, a pencil, and your thinking brain. There are 4 steps. Here is step one. Step 1. Read the story on your page. Sami made a frog game. He taps the frog... but nothing happens! Tell me in your own words: what did Sami WANT to happen when he tapped the frog?

games.label: Games
games.text:
Welcome to the Games page! 🎮

Here you play little quiz games about Unit 9. Each game has four quick questions with answers to pick from. We do this so the big words stick in your head — words like testing, error and debug. Games make practice fun. What I expect from you: read each question, pick your answer, and tell me why you picked it. Guessing is okay! Mistakes are how we learn. There are 12 games. We will do them one at a time. Step 1: On your screen, tap the first game. It is called "Quick Match: games developer". Tell me when it is open. 🙂

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today we are doing Computing Fluency. That means quick practice questions about our games developer words. We do it so the words become easy and fast for you — words like testing, error and Start on Tap. There are 6 little questions. I will give you one at a time. You just tell me your answer in your own words. Do not worry about being perfect — trying is what counts! You need only your voice or your typing. Ready? Here comes question one. What does testing mean? Is it eating your lunch, or trying your program to see if it works?

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text:
Hello! Today we are doing our Stay Safe Online activity. 🙂

This page has three safety rules for when we use a computer or tablet. We do it because a games developer works online, and we want you to be safe and happy there. By the end, you will be able to say all three rules in your own words. You need your listening ears, and a grown-up nearby if one is there. There are three steps — one rule each. Here comes step one. Rule one: Check before you trust. Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. If something is important, check it on another website, or ask a grown-up you trust. Now you try. Tell me in your own words: if you see something online, should you believe it straight away? Why or why not?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Solve Real Problems. Here is what we will do. You will look at little game problems and be the person who fixes them, just like a real games developer. We do this because making a game is easy — finding the mistake and fixing it is the real skill. By the end you will be able to spot a wrong block and say what it should be. What I expect from you: try each one yourself first, and answer in a full sentence if you can. Wrong answers are fine here. Mistakes are how we learn. You need only your eyes, your thinking, and the page in front of you. There are 4 problems, and I will give you one at a time. Here comes question one. Sami made a frog game. He wanted the frog to hop when he taps it. He tapped the frog... but nothing happened! His first block is Start on Green Flag. Tell me: is that the right block for a tap game? Why or why not?

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. Here is what we do. I ask you a question about our games. You do not just pick an answer — you tell me WHY, in your own words. Talking about our thinking helps it stick in our brain. By the end, you will be able to explain testing, errors and debugging like a real games developer. You need your voice and your brain. That's all! There are 4 questions. Here comes question one. In ScratchJr, which block makes the game start when you TAP the character? Tell me the block name, and then tell me how you know. 🐸

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Hello! Today you are a games developer — a person who makes computer games. In this project you will make your very own tap game in ScratchJr, then test it and fix it. Why? Because real games developers always try their game, find the mistakes, and fix them. That is the big skill of this unit. Here is what I expect from you: pick one character, make a plan, build it, tap it to test it, and stay happy even when something goes wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. You will need a tablet with ScratchJr, and paper and a pencil. There are 6 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Choose your character. Your character is the thing in your game. Pick one: frog, cat, dog or bird. Tell me which one you choose.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Welcome to your Unit Challenge! 🎮

This is where you become a real games developer — a person who makes computer games. You will make your very own tap game in ScratchJr. Then you will test it, find a bug, and fix it. By the end, you will have a game you can show your family and say "I made that!"

You need a tablet with ScratchJr, and a pencil and paper for planning. Ask your grown-up to help you open the app if you need to. There are 5 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Choose your character. Your character is the thing in your game. Pick a frog, a cat, a dog, or a bird — or draw your own. Tell me which one you picked!

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Unit 10: We Are Connected. This page is our map of the unit. We look at it first so you know what we will learn: how computers join together to share. By the end of this page, you will be able to say what a network is and name a few of our new words. All you need is your eyes, your voice, and a pencil if you like. There are 4 short steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Read the unit name out loud: "We Are Connected."
Now tell me, in your own words, what you think "connected" means. A good answer uses simple words like "joined" or "stuck together". Any guess is welcome!

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Today's lesson is called "We Are Connected". We will learn how computers join up and share. By the end, you will be able to say what a network is, and tell me what online and offline mean. All you need is your ears, your voice, and a pencil if you like drawing. There are 5 small steps. Here comes step one! Step 1: Picture one computer sitting all alone on a table. It cannot share anything with anyone. Now picture a second computer next to it, joined by a line. Tell me: when two computers are joined together, what do you think they can now do?

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Tools and Setup. This is where we get ready for Unit 10, "We Are Connected". The good news is easy: this unit needs no computer at all! We will draw and think with paper. Getting ready first means we never have to stop in the middle of a fun activity to go hunting for a pencil. By the end of this page, you will have everything on your table, ready to go. Here is what I expect from you: do each step, then tell me "done", and I will give you the next one. There are 3 small steps. Step 1: Go and get one sheet of paper and a pencil. If you have colour pencils or crayons, bring those too. You can ask your grown-up to help you find them. Tell me "done" when they are in your hands. 😊

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Welcome! Today we are learning the Computing Words for Unit 10, "We Are Connected". These are the special words that help us talk about how computers join up and share. By the end, you will be able to say each word, tell me what it means, and use it in your own sentence. You just need your voice and your thinking brain. A pencil and paper is nice too, but not needed. We will learn three words first. There are three steps. Step 1: our first word is connect. Connect means to join together. Like when you hold hands with a friend — you connect. Now you try. Tell me one thing at home that you can connect, or join together. Two Lego bricks? Two train tracks? Your idea!

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Welcome! Today we are doing "Join Them Up." It is our first Explore activity in the unit "We Are Connected."

Here is why we do it. Computers can share pictures and words — but only when they are joined together. When you join them, we call it a network. Drawing it helps you see it with your own eyes. By the end, you will be able to tell me what a network is, in your own words. You need a pencil and a sheet of paper (or your printed activity page). There are 3 short steps. I expect you to draw carefully and then tell me what you drew. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Near the left side of your paper, draw one computer. A simple box with a screen is perfect. Write "computer" under it if you like. Tell me when your first computer is drawn. 😊

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Visual Models page. 🙂

A visual model is a picture that shows an idea. On this page we will look at pictures of computers joining up. Doing this helps you SEE what a network is, so the words stick in your head. By the end you will be able to point at a picture and say what it shows. You need a pencil, a sheet of paper, and your talking voice. There are 5 steps — one for each picture. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Picture one is called "What is a network?"
On your paper, draw two little boxes. Each box is a computer. Now draw one straight line joining them. What I expect from you: two boxes, one line, and then tell me in your own words what those two joined computers are called. Take your time — there's no rush.

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Learn the Method". 🙂

This activity teaches you the way to think about a network. A network is two or more computers joined together. By the end, you will be able to make your own network on paper and say what it does. You need one sheet of paper and a pencil. There are four steps. I will give you one step at a time. Here is step 1. Say this idea back to me in your own words: what is a network? A good answer tells me two things — that computers are joined together, and that joined computers can share. Take your time. There is no rush.

code.label: Code Examples
code.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our lesson. On this page we look at a tiny picture made of letters and lines. It shows one computer, and then two computers joined together. We do it so you can SEE what the word network means. By the end, you will be able to point at the picture and tell me which one is a network. You need your eyes, your voice, and a pencil and paper if you have one. There are 3 steps. Here is step 1. Look at the first line on your page:

One computer: [Computer]

Read it out loud. Then tell me: how many computers do you see in that line? I am expecting a number, and one little reason, like "one, because there is only one box."

Take your time — there's no rush.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Welcome! Today we are on the Worked Examples page. A worked example is a question with the answer shown, so we can see how a good answer sounds. We do them so that later you can make good answers all by yourself. By the end, you will be able to say what a network is, and how things join with a wire or with no wire. You need your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like drawing. There are 6 examples. Here comes step one! Step one: look at Worked Example 1. It asks: which one can connect with no wire — a smartphone, or a brick? Tell me your answer, and tell me why you picked it. 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Welcome to Guided Practice! Here is what we are doing today. This page has six little questions about our unit, We Are Connected. We do them to make the big ideas stick — networks, wires, no wires, and the internet. By the end, you will be able to say what a network is and what online and offline mean. You just need your thinking brain and your voice. A pencil and paper is nice too. Here is what I expect from you: answer in a full sentence, not just one word. So instead of "network", say "Two or more computers joined together is a network." That is a Grade 1 star answer! Here comes question one. Two or more computers joined together is a... what? Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Build It
activities.text: Today we are going to build a network on paper. A network means two or more computers joined together so they can share. We do this so you can see with your own eyes what "joined together" looks like. By the end, you will be able to make a network and say what it is. You need a sheet of paper and a pencil. Your grown-up can help you if you like. There are 3 small steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Draw two computers, side by side, with a space in the middle. They can be simple boxes with a screen — nothing fancy! Tell me when your two computers are drawn. 😊

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are on the Quick Reference page for Unit 10, "We Are Connected". This page is our word box. It holds all the important words from this unit in one place, like network, wire and online. We do this so the words stick in your head, so you can use them when you talk about computers. By the end, you will be able to say each word and what it means, all by yourself. You just need your voice, and a pencil and paper if you like writing. Here is what I expect from you: say the meaning in your OWN words, not copied. Short is fine. A good answer is one that a friend would understand. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Our first word is network. A network is two or more computers joined together. Now you try — tell me what a network is, in your own words. 🙂

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Welcome to Debug It! In computing, "debug" means to find a mistake and fix it. On this page the mistakes are not in code — they are wrong ideas about networks and the internet. Why we do it: spotting a wrong idea helps you remember the right one much better. Here is what I expect from you. For each idea I read out, you tell me two things: is it right or wrong, and what would you say instead? A short answer in your own words is perfect. You just need your thinking voice — no pencil needed. There are six ideas to check. Let's start with something small. Step 1. Someone says: "A network is a kind of computer."

Is that right or wrong? Tell me what you think. 🙂

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today we are doing Computing Fluency. Fluency means answering quickly, because the words are getting comfy in your head. There are 6 short questions about networks and the internet. They are all from what you already learned in this unit. You don't need anything special — just your voice or your typing hands. Here is what I expect from you: try each one, and say your answer in a full sentence if you can. It is fine to be wrong. Mistakes are how we learn. Here comes question one. Two or more computers joined together is called a... what?

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our Games page for Unit 10, We Are Connected. The games are little challenges about joining computers together. We play them so the big words — network, wire, internet, online, offline — stick in your head like a favourite song. By the end you will be able to say what a network is and how devices join up. What I expect from you: try your best guess out loud or type it, even if you are not sure. Guessing bravely is how we learn. You need nothing but your thinking brain! 😊

There are 4 rounds in our first game. Here comes question one. Round 1: Two or more computers joined together — what do we call that? Take your time — there's no rush.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Welcome! Today we are doing "Solve Real Problems". This activity gives you little real-life moments — at home, at school, at the market — and you use what you know about networks and the internet to answer. We do it because knowing a word is good, but using it in real life is even better. By the end, you will be able to say when we are online, when we are offline, and what a network is. You need your thinking brain and your voice. A pencil and paper if you like. There are 4 questions. Here comes question one. At home, Mum's tablet is joined to the internet. Finish this sentence: "When our device is joined to the internet, we are ______."

I am looking for one word, and then say the whole sentence back to me. Take your time — there's no rush.

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Welcome! Today we are on Stay Safe Online. The internet joins us to people all around the world. That is lovely — but we need safe rules, just like crossing the road. There are four safety rules to learn. By the end, you will be able to say each rule in your own words. You need your listening ears, and a pencil and paper if you like. Step 1 of 4: Keep your private things private. Your full name, your address, your school, your phone number and your passwords are called personal information. They belong to you. We never type them into a game or a website, and we never send them to someone we only met online. Here is what I expect from you: tell me one thing from that list that you would keep private. Just one. 😊

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Explain Your Thinking."

In this activity you do not just give an answer — you say WHY. That is the fun part. Talking about why helps the idea stick in your brain, and it shows me what you understand about networks and the internet. There are 4 questions. You need your thinking voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want help typing. What I expect from you: give your answer, then add "because..." with one reason. Even a short reason is great. Here comes question one. A smartphone and a brick are on the table. Which one can connect with no wire — and why?

project.label: Unit Project
project.text: Welcome to your Unit Project! Today you are going to make one big piece of work called "We Are Connected". You will draw a network with wires, then draw devices that need no wire, and then answer one question about online and offline. We do this so you can show everything you learned in this unit — all in one place. When you finish, you will be able to point at your paper and explain how computers join up and share. You need one sheet of paper, a pencil, and colours if you have them. There are 5 small steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Draw two computers and one printer on your paper. Just the boxes and shapes — no lines yet. A good drawing here has three separate things, spread out with space between them, so we have room for the wires later. Tell me when your three things are drawn! 🖍️

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Welcome to your Unit Challenge! This is where you show everything you learned about being connected. You will make one piece of work: your own network drawing. By the end, you will be able to show a network with wires, show devices with no wire, and say what online and offline mean. You need a sheet of paper, a pencil, and some colours if you have them. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 5 steps. I will give you one at a time. 🙂

Step 1: Draw two computers and one printer on your paper. Then draw lines between them — those lines are the wires. What I want to see: three things drawn, and lines joining them so they can share. That is your network! Tell me when you have done it.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Welcome to Unit 11, Be an Artist! 🎨

Here is what this unit is about. We will learn to draw pictures by giving directions, like up, down, left and right. Artists draw with a pencil. Computers draw the same way — by following steps in order. By the end, you will draw a square all by yourself, and move a bee in ScratchJr. For today you need a pencil, some paper, and your two arms ready to point! There are 4 steps in our overview. Here comes step one. Step 1: The four directions. Stand up if you can. Point your arm UP to the ceiling. Now point DOWN to the floor. Now point LEFT. Now point RIGHT. I expect you to try all four with your arm, and say each word out loud as you point. Tell me when you have done it. Which one felt the trickiest?

tools.label: Tools & Setup
tools.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are getting our art tool ready. 🎨

This activity is called Tools and Setup. We are going to open ScratchJr. ScratchJr is a free app where you join little blocks to make a character move. By the end, you will have a new project open and ready, so next time we can make a bee walk to a flower. What you need: a tablet with the ScratchJr app, and a grown-up nearby to help you tap. What I expect from you: try each step yourself, then tell me what you see on the screen. If something looks different, just say so. That is helpful, not wrong! There are 4 steps. Here is step 1. Step 1: Find the ScratchJr app on your tablet and tap it to open it. A good job looks like this: the app opens and you see a picture screen with a little cat. Tell me when it is open, or tell me what you see.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and our lesson is called Be an Artist. We will learn the four directions — up, down, left and right — and use them to draw a shape. Artists draw with their hands. Computers draw by following directions, one step at a time. By the end, you will draw a square all by yourself, just by following arrows. You need a pencil, a piece of paper, and your arms ready to point. There are five steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Stand up if you can. Point your arm UP to the sky. Now point DOWN to the floor. Now point LEFT. Now point RIGHT. I expect you to say all four out loud as you point: up, down, left, right. Tell me when you have done it! 🙂

words.label: Computing Words
words.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Computing Words page. These are the special words we use in Unit 11, "Be an Artist". We learn them so you can talk about drawing shapes with directions, just like a real computer artist. By the end you will know each word and be able to use it in your own sentence. You need your ears, your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. There are three parts. In each part we learn three words. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Our first word is direction. A direction is which way something moves. Up, down, left and right are directions. Now you try: point your arm up. Then point it down. Then tell me one more direction you know.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and our activity is called Meet the Arrows. In this activity we look at the four directions: up, down, left and right. We do it because computers only move when we tell them which way to go. By the end, you will be able to point to an arrow and show that direction with your arm. You need a pencil, a piece of paper, and your own two arms. There are 4 short steps. Step 1: Draw four arrows on your paper. One pointing up, one pointing down, one pointing left, and one pointing right. A good arrow has a straight line and a little pointy tip. Tell me when your four arrows are drawn.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are going to look at the Picture Models for Unit 11. A picture model is a small picture that shows one big idea. We use them because pictures help our brains remember. By the end, you will be able to show all four arrows, follow a path, and draw a square with steps. You need a pencil, some paper, and your arm for pointing. There are 5 steps, and I will give you one at a time. Step 1: The four directions. Point your arm up. Then down. Then left. Then right. Then tell me: which direction is your hand going when you point to the floor? 👇

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing "Learn the Method". A method is just a way of working. Ours is about the four directions: up, down, left and right. By the end, you will be able to say a direction, copy an example, and check if you were right — like a real artist and a real programmer. You need a pencil, some paper, and your arms ready to point! There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: Say the main idea in your own words. Tell me: what does the word direction mean? A good answer is something like "which way something moves". Say it your way. I'm listening! 😊

code.label: Code Examples
code.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Code Examples. Code examples are short lists of arrow steps, like little recipes for drawing and moving. We read them so we learn to think like a computer: one step, then the next step, in order. By the end you will be able to read a short list of arrows and say what it draws. You need your arm to point with, a pencil, and some paper. 🙂

Here is what I expect from you: read each line out loud, point your arm the way the arrow points, and tell me what you think happens. There are 5 little lists on this page. Let's start with number one. Step 1. Read this list out loud, slowly, and point your arm each time:

Up (this is forward)
Down (this is backward)
Left
Right

When you have said all four and pointed all four, tell me "done".

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a question with the thinking shown, so we can learn how to do it. We are doing this so you can draw and move things by giving directions — like a real artist and a real programmer! You will need a pencil, some paper, and your voice to tell me your answers. There are 3 steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1: On your paper, draw four arrows — one pointing up, one down, one left, and one right. Then point your arm the same way for each one. I expect you to draw all four and say each direction out loud: up, down, left, right. Tell me when you are done! 😊

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice in "Be an Artist". In this activity we practise giving directions — up, down, left and right — and using them to draw a shape. We do it because a computer can only draw when we give it steps in the right order. By the end, you will know your four arrows, and how many corners a square has, and how to put steps in order. You need a pencil and paper. And your arms, for pointing! There are 4 short steps. I will give you one at a time. Here comes step one. Draw four arrows on your paper: one pointing up, one down, one left, one right. Then point your arm the same way as each one. I expect you to tell me: which arrow points up — is it the one pointing to the sky, or to the floor?

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are working on the Quick Reference page of Unit 11, Be an Artist. Quick Reference is our little word card. It holds all the important words for this unit, like direction, arrow and algorithm. We go through it so those words stick in your head, and so you can use them when you draw shapes with steps. By the end you will be able to say the four directions, and explain three unit words in your own words. You need: a pencil, some paper, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: The four directions. Say them out loud and point with your arm each time: up, down, left, right. What I expect: you point four times, and you tell me the four direction words back to me. Off you go — tell me when you have done it!

activities.label: Build It
activities.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are going to be artists with arrows. 🎨

This activity is called Meet the Arrows. We learn the four directions: up, down, left and right. Each one has its own arrow. We do this because arrows are how we tell a computer which way to move — later we will use them to draw a whole shape! What I expect from you: point with your arm, say the direction out loud, and tell me when you are done. There is no rush. You need a pencil and paper (or your activity page). There are 4 steps. Step 1: Draw an arrow pointing up on your paper. Like an arrow flying to the sky. Then point your arm up and say "up!"

Tell me when you have done it. 😊

debug.label: Debug It
debug.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Debug It. A bug is a small mistake in our steps. Debugging means finding the mistake and fixing it. We do this because every artist and every programmer makes mistakes — that is normal! By the end, you will be able to spot a wrong step and fix it all by yourself. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your two hands ready to point. We have four little bugs to fix, and I will give you one at a time. Here comes bug number one. Someone says: "Left and right are the same."

Is that true or not true? Tell me your answer, and then point your arm to the left for me. 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to your Games page! This is the fun part of Unit 11. These games are quick practice. Each game gives you four little questions about directions, arrows, steps and shapes. Playing them helps the words stick in your brain, so you can be an artist who draws with directions. Here is what I expect from you: pick an answer, tell me your pick, and say why you chose it. Guessing is okay. Mistakes are how we learn. You need nothing but your eyes and your voice. There are 12 games, but we will start with just the first one. Step 1: On your screen, find the game called "Quick Match: direction" and tap it to start. Tell me when it opens. 🙂

fluency.label: Computing Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. Let's do Computing Fluency together. Fluency means quick practice. We answer short questions fast, so the ideas stick in our head — like practising a song until you know it. There are four rounds. One question each time. I expect you to try first, say your answer in a short sentence, and tell me if you get stuck. There is no rush. You need a pencil and paper nearby. Ready? Here comes question one. Look at these three arrows:

A) ^
B) v
C) >

Which one points up?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher today. Let's do this activity together. 😊

This page is called Solve Real Problems. It has four little questions about directions and shapes — one about home, one about school, one about a market, and one about your community. We do this so you can use what you learned about arrows, steps and shapes in real life, not just on the page. Here is what I expect from you: answer in your own words, in a full sentence if you can, and take your time. Wrong answers are fine — we fix them together. You will need a pencil and paper nearby. There are 4 steps, one question each. Here comes question one. Question 1 (Home): To draw a shape, we follow a list of ______. Think about how we drew the square window. What did we follow, one after the other? Tell me your word.

safety.label: Stay Safe Online
safety.text: Welcome! Today we are learning how to stay safe online. This is our Stay Safe Online page. We do this because computers and the internet are fun, but we need safe habits — just like we look both ways before we cross the road. By the end, you will know three safety rules and be able to say them in your own words. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if one is close. There are three steps, one for each rule. Step 1. The first rule is: check before you trust. Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. If it is important, check it on a second website, and ask a grown-up you trust. Here is what I expect from you: tell me one thing you could do if you read something online and you are not sure it is true.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is called Explain Your Thinking. Here you say ideas in your own words. Not just the right answer — the why behind it. This helps the ideas stick in your head, and it makes you a real thinker, like an artist explaining her picture. You will need your pencil and paper, or you can just tell me out loud. There are four short questions. I will give you one at a time. Here comes question one. Put these steps in the right order. Write 1, 2, 3 next to them:

Move right
Stop program
Start program

I expect three numbers from you, and then one little sentence saying why. Take your time — there's no rush.

challenge.label: Unit Challenge
challenge.text:
Hello! Today you are the artist. 🎨

Here is our challenge: you will draw a square window by following direction steps. Then you will find a wrong step in a list and fix it. We do this because computers draw pictures the same way — by following steps in the right order. What you need: paper and a pencil. What I expect: you follow one step at a time, and you tell me when each one is done. Mistakes are fine — we fix them together. There are 5 steps. Here is step 1. Take your paper. Put four dots to make a square shape, like the corners of a window. Top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left. Tell me when your four dots are ready.

project.label: Unit Project
project.text:
Hello! Today you are the artist, and I am your teacher. 🎨

This is our Unit Project: Be an Artist. You will draw a square window by following direction steps. Then you will look at a set of steps that has one wrong step, find it, and fix it. We do this because a computer draws pictures the very same way — it follows one small step at a time, in order. Here is what I expect from you: use your pencil, go one step at a time, and say "done" when you finish each step. If a step goes wrong, that is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. Get a pencil and a piece of paper. There are 5 steps. Step 1: Draw four dots on your paper to make the corners of a square. One dot top left, one dot top right, one dot bottom right, one dot bottom left. Leave a space between them, about as wide as your thumb. Tell me "done" when your four dots are ready.
